title: Business Strategy & Competitive Advantage
theme: Thinking Like a General Manager and Chief Strategy Officer
question: What makes an organization’s advantage defensible, and how should scarce resources be committed when rivals adapt and the future is uncertain?

overview.text: Weeks 5 to 8 dealt with people: how leaders influence, negotiate and design organizations. This week steps back to the question a general manager or chief strategy officer must answer before any of that matters: where will this organization be distinctively good, who will capture the value it creates, and what will it give up to get there? Strategy, in the sense used here, is not a vision statement or a list of goals. It is a coherent set of choices about scarce resources in the presence of rivals who are making choices too.

The four lessons build one argument. Lesson 1 separates strategy from operational improvement and from goals, using Porter’s account of positioning and trade-offs and Rumelt’s kernel of diagnosis, guiding policy and coherent action. Lesson 2 looks outward at industry structure and value capture — the five forces, value-based strategy and the evidence on how much industry matters. Lesson 3 looks inward at resources and capabilities, the critique that the resource-based view is circular, and the practical decision of whether to build or buy. Lesson 4 asks how long any advantage lasts, using evidence that a mispriced skill in baseball’s labor market was priced away once it became public, and how to commit resources under uncertainty.

The week is deliberately skeptical about its own tools. Most strategy frameworks are conceptual arguments or practitioner heuristics, not tested models, and the strongest large-sample evidence describes associations rather than causes. You will learn to use the frameworks as disciplined questions — what are we refusing, what do we add that others cannot, what will still be ours once rivals copy us — rather than as answers. The Strategy Table exercise and the Ferrovane Labs case then put those questions under the pressure of a fixed budget and an uncertain future, and the strategy memo asks you to write the choices down, including what will stop.

objectives: Distinguish strategy from operational effectiveness and from goals, and rewrite an aspiration as a strategy kernel.
Analyze how industry structure and added value determine who captures the value an organization creates.
Evaluate resources and capabilities with the VRIN criteria, including the tautology critique, and apply them to build-versus-buy decisions.
Explain why information-based advantages erode, using evidence from a professional sports labor market, and identify advantages that erode more slowly.
Allocate scarce resources coherently under a chosen strategy and across scenarios, and diagnose peanut-butter allocation.

lessons.title: What Strategy Is — and What It Is Not
lessons.summary: Strategy is a coherent set of choices about how to create distinctive value, which means accepting trade-offs and deciding what not to do; it is neither operational excellence nor a list of goals.
objectives: Distinguish operational effectiveness from strategic positioning and explain why only the second can sustain an advantage.
Explain how trade-offs and fit among activities make a position hard to imitate.
Diagnose a statement of goals or aspirations and rewrite it as a strategy kernel: diagnosis, guiding policy and coherent actions.
lessons.executive: Most documents called “strategy” are lists of goals, values and improvement programs. Porter’s distinction lets you test them: operational effectiveness — doing the same things better — is necessary but easy to copy, so it rarely sustains an advantage. Strategy is choosing a distinctive position, accepting the trade-offs that come with it, and building activities that reinforce one another. Rumelt adds a practical test: a strategy names the critical challenge, sets a guiding policy and commits coherent actions. If a plan does not say what to stop doing or whom to turn away, treat it as an aspiration. Mintzberg adds a warning: the strategy you actually have is the pattern in what you do and fund.

explore.text: A regional health system publishes its five-year plan. Its strategy, the document says, is “to be the most trusted provider of world-class care in the region, through clinical excellence, innovation, a culture of caring and operational efficiency.” Beneath that sentence sit thirty-one initiatives, each with an owner, a budget line and a dashboard. The board approves the plan unanimously. Nobody objects, because there is nothing in it to object to.

Before reading on: name one thing this plan tells the health system to stop doing, or one kind of patient, service or partner it tells the system to turn away. If you cannot, what does that tell you about the plan?

The honest answer is usually “nothing”. The plan lists desirable outcomes and worthy activities; it does not choose. A competitor reading it would learn nothing about where the system intends to be hard to beat, and a department head reading it could find a justification for almost any budget request. This lesson argues that this is the most common failure in strategic work: the absence of choice dressed up as ambition.

The pattern appears far from hospitals. A software company “aims to be the leading platform for every customer segment”. A law firm commits to “full-service excellence”. A government agency promises to “modernize, innovate and deliver value for taxpayers”. A professional sports organization wants to “win now and build for the future”. Each statement may be sincere. None tells you what the organization will do differently from its rivals, or what it will give up in order to do it.

Two scholars supply the sharpest tools for telling a real strategy from its imitations. Michael Porter separates strategy from operational improvement. Richard Rumelt separates strategy from goals. A third, Henry Mintzberg, complicates both by asking whether strategy is something leaders decide in advance or something an organization reveals in its own behavior. By the end of the lesson you should be able to take any plan you are handed and ask three questions of it: where is it distinctive, what problem does it solve, and what does it refuse?

understand.text: Operational effectiveness is not strategy

Porter’s 1996 essay begins with a distinction most executives skip. **Operational effectiveness** means performing similar activities better than rivals: faster cycle times, fewer defects, lower costs, better use of technology. **Strategic positioning** means performing *different* activities from rivals, or performing similar activities in *different ways*, so that the organization delivers a distinctive mix of value. Porter argues that operational effectiveness is necessary for superior performance but not sufficient, because its techniques diffuse quickly. Benchmarking, consultants and best-practice networks spread every improvement across an industry. The result is what he calls competitive convergence: rivals become more alike, and the gains from their improvements flow to customers and suppliers rather than to any one firm.

understand.text: Positions, trade-offs and fit

A position, in Porter’s account, can rest on serving a particular *variety* of products or services, on serving most of the *needs* of a particular group of customers, or on serving customers who differ in how they can be *accessed* — by geography, scale or channel. A position becomes defensible only when it involves **trade-offs**: choices where more of one thing means less of another. Trade-offs arise because activities that suit one position do not suit another, because a reputation for one kind of value is hard to combine with a reputation for its opposite, and because an organization cannot coordinate and control incompatible activities well. Porter’s illustrations include a low-fare airline that deliberately offered no meals, no assigned seats and no baggage transfers to other carriers, and a furniture retailer whose customers collect and assemble their own furniture. Each choice that lowers cost for the specialist would be a defect for a rival serving a different customer.

Trade-offs explain why imitation is hard. A rival that copies some activities without accepting the trade-offs ends up **straddling**: carrying the costs of two positions and the advantages of neither. Porter describes a full-service airline that launched a low-fare service on some routes while keeping its full-service apparatus elsewhere; the hybrid matched neither the specialist’s costs nor its own service standard. Copying a competitor’s visible practices is easy; copying the choices that make those practices pay is not.

The final element is **fit**: the way activities reinforce one another. Porter distinguishes simple consistency between each activity and the overall strategy, activities that actively reinforce each other, and coordination that optimizes effort across the whole system. Fit matters for defense. A competitor can copy any single practice, but the value lies in the system, and matching a whole system is far harder than matching one part of it. In Porter’s formulation, the essence of strategy is choosing what not to do.

A simple calculation shows why systems protect. Suppose a rival has a 90% chance of successfully copying any one of your activities, and the attempts are independent. The chance it copies two linked activities is 0.9 × 0.9 = 0.81. For ten mutually reinforcing activities the chance falls to about 0.35. The numbers are illustrative, not empirical, but the logic is robust: when value depends on the combination, the probabilities of successful imitation multiply.

understand.text: The kernel of a good strategy

Rumelt, writing from decades of consulting and teaching, offers a complementary test that works at any level of an organization. A good strategy has a **kernel** of three parts. The **diagnosis** names and explains the critical challenge — the obstacle that, once overcome, unlocks progress. The **guiding policy** is the overall approach to that challenge; it channels and constrains action without specifying every step. **Coherent actions** are coordinated commitments of resources and policy that carry out the guiding policy and reinforce one another. Rumelt also catalogues the hallmarks of bad strategy: fluff (grand language that restates the obvious), failure to face the challenge, mistaking goals for strategy, and strategic objectives that are either a jumble of unrelated items or as hard as the original problem.

The two frameworks meet in a single idea: strategy is the disciplined use of scarce resources against a specific problem. Porter asks where you will be distinctive and what you will give up. Rumelt asks what problem you are solving and whether your actions concentrate on it.

understand.title: Prerequisite: opportunity cost — the price of every yes

blocks.text: Economists define the **opportunity cost** of a choice as the value of the best alternative you give up by making it. A department’s budget, its leaders’ attention and its best people can each be spent only once. When a plan funds thirty-one initiatives, the opportunity cost of each is the stronger version of the others that the organization could have built with the same resources.

Two consequences follow. First, an initiative can be worthwhile on its own merits and still be a poor choice, if the alternative use of the same money or talent is better. Second, resources that look free are rarely free. An analyst with “spare capacity”, a facility that is “already paid for” and a leader’s “extra” afternoon all have alternative uses. The question is never only “Is this good?” but “Is this better than what we would do instead?” [Week 10](#w10) builds the financial version of this logic.

understand.title: Methodological note: how do we know any of this works?

blocks.text: Neither Porter’s essay nor Rumelt’s book is a statistical test. Both argue from theory and from carefully chosen cases. That is a legitimate way to build concepts, but it has known weaknesses. The examples are usually organizations that succeeded, so we rarely see the ones that made equally sharp trade-offs and failed — survivorship bias. The counterfactual is unobserved: we cannot know how the low-fare airline would have fared with a different strategy. And success stories are told after the fact, when a lucky sequence of decisions is easy to describe as a coherent plan.

Treat these frameworks as **disciplined questions**, not validated laws. They are most useful for exposing incoherence — a plan with no trade-offs, actions that contradict each other, a missing diagnosis — and least reliable as predictions of which strategy will win. Large-sample research on strategy has the opposite problem: it can measure profitability across thousands of firms, but it struggles to measure “fit” or “quality of diagnosis” directly. Lesson 2 shows what that research can and cannot tell you.

challenge.text: Plan or pattern?

Mintzberg and Waters drew a distinction that unsettles the idea of strategy as a choice made at the top. An **intended** strategy is what leaders plan. A **realized** strategy is the pattern that actually appears in the organization’s stream of actions. Intended strategies that are realized are **deliberate**; intended strategies that are not realized are **unrealized**; and patterns that were never intended but appear anyway are **emergent**. They argued that purely deliberate and purely emergent strategies are the two ends of a continuum, and that real strategies lie between them — for example, an “umbrella” strategy in which leaders set broad boundaries and let the specifics emerge from people closer to the work.

The two traditions disagree about where good strategy comes from. The positioning view emphasizes deliberate analysis and commitment: choose a position, accept trade-offs, build fit. The emergent view emphasizes learning: organizations often discover what works by acting, and insisting on detailed plans can blind leaders to patterns their own people are already finding. Neither side has a decisive empirical win; the disagreement is about which risk is larger in a given setting — drift and incoherence without deliberate choice, or rigidity and blindness with too much of it. A practical synthesis is to decide deliberately on the few commitments that are costly to reverse, and to treat the rest as experiments whose results are allowed to change the plan.

Trade-offs are not permanent either. New technology can move the frontier so that an organization gets more of two things at once: online banking lowered cost and raised convenience; telemedicine extended access without new clinics. When the frontier moves, positions built on yesterday’s trade-offs can become vulnerable, and an incumbent that defends them too long can be overtaken. The right response is not to abandon the idea of trade-offs but to re-examine which ones still bind after the technology has changed.

Rumelt’s kernel deserves the same skepticism as any practitioner framework. It is a useful checklist derived from experience, not a tested model. There is no study showing that organizations whose plans contain a diagnosis outperform those that do not, and such a study would be hard to design. Its value is that each element can be inspected: a diagnosis can be wrong, a guiding policy can be vague, actions can contradict each other. That is more than can be said for a vision statement, which cannot be wrong because it does not say anything.

Finally, not every organization competes in the commercial sense. A public agency, a university department or a player-development system does not face rivals for customers in the way an airline does. The logic still applies: each competes for scarce resources, talent and results relative to peers, and each must decide where to concentrate — with “value” meaning outcomes for citizens, students or players rather than profit.

apply.text: Worked example: from aspiration to kernel

Return to the health system. Suppose the analysis behind the plan shows three facts (all synthetic): its emergency departments hold admitted patients for long periods because inpatient beds are occupied by patients waiting for discharge to rehabilitation and long-term care; its specialty surgery lines lose money because operating rooms start late and cancel often; and a national competitor is opening outpatient clinics in the wealthiest suburbs. A kernel might read as follows.

apply.text: Notice three features. The diagnosis is a claim about causes that could be wrong and can be checked. The guiding policy rules out attractive options. The actions concentrate resources where the diagnosis says the constraint lies, and the list of what stops is as concrete as the list of what starts.

Now a different setting. A mid-sized litigation firm finds that a growing share of partner time goes to low-margin document review, while a handful of regulatory clients generate most of its profit. Its aspiration is “full-service excellence”. A kernel would name the challenge (partner time is consumed by work clients will not pay premium rates for), adopt a guiding policy (concentrate on complex regulatory matters where judgment commands a premium), and commit coherent actions (refer or outsource high-volume review, recruit two regulatory specialists, reprice the remaining work). Each action implies a refusal, and the firm will lose some clients it currently serves. That loss is the price of the position.

In player development the same discipline applies to a department’s philosophy. A statement that commits to “individualized development for every player, cutting-edge technology, elite coaching and a winning culture” lists goods without choosing among them. A kernel would identify the binding constraint — for example, that skilled coaching hours per player at the lower levels are the scarcest input — and set a guiding policy such as concentrating individualized programming where the evidence suggests marginal hours matter most, with standardized plans elsewhere. The coherent actions would follow from that policy, and so would an explicit list of programs to retire.

apply.title: Executive twist: the board wants targets, not a diagnosis

blocks.text: Your board or ownership group asks for “a strategy” and expects growth targets, a list of initiatives and a confident tone. You believe the honest diagnosis is that one constraint dominates and that several popular programs should end. Your evidence for the constraint is internal data and the judgment of experienced staff, not a controlled comparison. How do you present a kernel to people who asked for a vision? You could lead with targets and embed the diagnosis, lead with the diagnosis and translate it into targets, or present two scenarios and ask for a choice. Each option carries a different risk to your credibility if the diagnosis turns out to be wrong — and a different risk to the organization if it is right and ignored.

retain.text: Strategy is choice under scarcity. Operational effectiveness is necessary but copyable; a defensible position rests on trade-offs and on activities that reinforce each other. Rumelt’s kernel turns that idea into a test — diagnosis, guiding policy, coherent actions — and Mintzberg adds that the strategy an organization actually has is the pattern in what it does and funds, whatever the plan says.

A defensible position requires trade-offs — choices that would be mistakes for a rival serving a different customer — and fit among activities.
A strategy kernel names the critical challenge, sets a guiding policy and commits coherent actions; goals and slogans are not strategy.
Every yes has an opportunity cost: the best alternative use of the same money, talent and attention.
Realized strategy is the pattern in what an organization actually does, which can differ sharply from its stated plan.

check.prompt: A logistics company adopts the same route-optimization software, warehouse automation and lean practices as its three main rivals and cuts its costs by 12%. Two years later its margins are back where they started. Which idea from Porter most directly explains this?

options.text: A failure of execution: the improvements were never fully implemented.
Competitive convergence: the improvements diffused across rivals, and the gains passed to customers.
Straddling: the company tried to occupy two positions at once.
Emergent strategy: the company’s realized strategy differed from its intended one.

check.explanation: The company improved operational effectiveness using practices its rivals also adopted. When everyone improves in the same way, relative position does not change and competition passes the savings to customers. Porter calls this competitive convergence; it is why operational effectiveness is necessary but not sufficient.

optionFeedback.a: Nothing in the vignette suggests poor implementation; costs did fall by 12%. The problem is that rivals made the same improvements.
optionFeedback.c: Straddling means trying to serve two incompatible positions. Here the company did not change position at all; it improved the same activities as everyone else.
optionFeedback.d: There is no sign of a gap between intended and realized strategy. The issue is that the improvements were imitable.

check.prompt: Which of the following are hallmarks of bad strategy in Rumelt’s account? Select all that apply.

Failing to identify and face the critical challenge
A guiding policy that rules out some attractive options

check.explanation: Rumelt lists fluff, failure to face the challenge, mistaking goals for strategy and poorly chosen strategic objectives as hallmarks of bad strategy. A guiding policy that rules out attractive options and actions that reinforce each other are features of good strategy: they show that choices have been made and that resources are concentrated.

check.prompt: Which description best fits the company’s realized strategy?

stimulus.text: A software company’s plan commits it to selling to large enterprises. Over three years, however, its sales team keeps closing small deals with mid-sized firms because they buy faster, and engineering builds features those customers request. By year three, 70% of revenue comes from mid-sized firms, and the enterprise plan has quietly stalled. (Fictional.)

options.text: A deliberate strategy, because the leadership approved the plan.
An emergent strategy: a realized pattern of serving mid-sized firms that was never intended, while the intended enterprise strategy went unrealized.
Operational effectiveness, because the sales team was efficient.
No strategy at all, because the plan was not followed.

check.explanation: Mintzberg and Waters define realized strategy as the pattern in an organization’s actions. Here the pattern — serving mid-sized firms — was not intended, so it is emergent, and the intended enterprise strategy is unrealized. Whether the emergent pattern is a good one is a separate question that leadership should now answer deliberately.

optionFeedback.a: Approval makes a strategy intended, not deliberate. A deliberate strategy is one that is both intended and realized; this one was not realized.
optionFeedback.c: Efficiency in closing deals is operational; the question asks about the pattern of where the company competes.
optionFeedback.d: There is a strategy — a clear, consistent pattern. It is simply not the one that was planned.

lessons.title: Industry Structure and Value Capture
lessons.summary: Creating value and capturing it are different problems: industry structure shapes how value is divided, and a firm can keep only what it adds that others cannot.
objectives: Use the five forces to explain why average profitability differs across industries and to identify the force that matters most in a given market.
Calculate value created and a firm’s added value, and explain why added value limits what a firm can capture.
Interpret evidence on how much industry and firm-specific factors each explain of profitability, and state the limits of that evidence.
lessons.executive: Value created is not value captured. Porter’s five forces — entry, supplier power, buyer power, substitutes and rivalry — explain how an industry’s structure divides the value it creates, which is why some industries earn persistently more than others. Brandenburger and Stuart sharpen the point for a single firm: value created is customers’ willingness to pay minus suppliers’ opportunity cost, and a firm can capture no more than its added value — what would be lost if it disappeared. Large-sample evidence suggests both industry and firm matter, with firm-specific effects larger on average. Before celebrating what you create, ask who can take it away.

explore.text: Commercial aviation is a standard puzzle in strategy teaching. The value of air travel to passengers is immense, and airlines move enormous numbers of people. Yet airlines have long been the textbook example of an industry whose structure keeps returns low, while some of the firms that supply them have done considerably better. The value is created in the act of flying; much of it is captured elsewhere — by passengers through low fares, and by suppliers with stronger bargaining positions.
Before reading on: list three reasons why an industry that creates great value for its customers might still earn poor returns. Then ask whether any of them describe a market you know well.

A second puzzle comes from technology. A start-up builds a tool that saves hospitals thousands of staff hours a year. Customers love it. But three competitors offer similar tools, hospitals can switch at each annual renewal, and the cloud provider that hosts the software raises its prices every year. The start-up creates a great deal of value and keeps very little of it. Its problem is not its product. It is its position in the structure of the market.

This lesson separates two questions executives often merge. **Value creation** asks how much better off customers, suppliers and the firm are because an activity exists. **Value capture** asks who ends up with that value. A strategy that answers only the first question produces grateful customers and an exhausted organization. The tools in this lesson — five forces, the value line and added value — answer the second. They apply as much to a hospital negotiating with a software vendor, or a sports organization competing for coaches, as to a manufacturer choosing a market.

understand.text: The five forces

Porter’s framework, first published in 1979 and restated in 2008, holds that the average profitability of an industry is shaped by five forces: the **threat of new entrants**, the **bargaining power of suppliers**, the **bargaining power of buyers**, the **threat of substitute** products or services, and the intensity of **rivalry** among existing competitors. Strong forces push returns down. Powerful buyers bargain prices down; powerful suppliers push input costs up; easy entry and close substitutes cap the price customers will pay; intense rivalry, especially on price, transfers value to customers. The strongest force or forces matter most, and they differ from industry to industry.

understand.text: Porter is careful about what the framework does not include. Industry growth, technology, government policy and complementary products are **factors, not forces**: they matter through their effect on the five forces. Rapid growth, for example, does not guarantee profits if it attracts entrants and strengthens suppliers. He also warns against defining an industry too broadly or too narrowly, and against listing forces without asking how they are shifting and where a firm can position itself so that the strongest forces bite least.
Value-based strategy and added value

Brandenburger and Stuart offered a complementary lens built on cooperative game theory. Picture a vertical line. At the top is the customer’s **willingness to pay**: the most a customer would pay rather than go without. At the bottom is the supplier’s **opportunity cost**: the least a supplier would accept to provide its inputs. The distance between them is the **value created**. Price and cost then divide it: customers keep willingness to pay minus price, the firm keeps price minus cost, and suppliers keep cost minus their opportunity cost. The analysis gives buyers and suppliers equal standing, so a firm can create value either by raising customers’ willingness to pay or by lowering its suppliers’ opportunity cost — for instance, by being an easier or more attractive customer to supply.

items.label: Firm’s cost (paid to suppliers and staff)

understand.note: Synthetic example. Value created = 500 − 120 = 380; the customer keeps 200, the firm keeps 120, suppliers keep 60.

understand.text: The central concept is **added value**: the value created by all the players together minus the value that would be created if one particular player were removed. Brandenburger and Stuart show that, under their assumptions, a firm cannot capture more than its added value. If a rival could deliver almost the same value without you, your added value is small, and no amount of negotiating skill will let you keep much. Positive added value requires an **asymmetry** between you and your rivals — something you do that they cannot.

Use the synthetic contract above to see the arithmetic. Suppose the customer’s next-best alternative is a rival product it values at $420,000 a year, and the rival’s suppliers and staff would accept $150,000. With you, the system creates 500 − 120 = $380,000 of value; without you, it creates 420 − 150 = $270,000. Your added value is $110,000. If the rival competes hard and prices down to its cost, the customer can get $270,000 of surplus elsewhere, so you must leave it at least that much: your price can be at most $230,000, and your margin at most $110,000. Today’s $120,000 margin depends on the rival not competing hard. Added value tells you how much of today’s profit is defensible.

understand.title: Prerequisite: economic profit and why average returns converge

blocks.text: Accounting profit is revenue minus recorded costs. **Economic profit** also subtracts the opportunity cost of the capital tied up in the business — what investors could have earned elsewhere at similar risk. A firm can report accounting profits and still destroy economic value if its returns fall below its cost of capital.

In a market without barriers, economic profits attract imitators and entrants until returns fall toward the cost of capital; losses drive exit until returns rise toward it. In economic terms, strategy is the search for reasons this convergence will not happen to you: structural barriers in the industry, or asymmetries in the firm. Week 10 develops the cost-of-capital idea in detail.

understand.text: How much does industry matter?

If industry structure shapes profitability, how much of the difference between business units is explained by the industry they are in, and how much by the unit itself? McGahan and Porter (1997) decomposed the variance in business-unit profitability across U.S. industries. They attributed roughly 19% of the variance to industry effects, 32% to business-specific effects, 4% to the corporate parent and 2% to year effects. Industry effects were smaller in manufacturing and larger in service sectors such as lodging and entertainment, wholesale and retail trade, and transportation.

understand.caption: Share of variance in business-unit profitability attributed to each effect
understand.note: Rounded figures reported by McGahan and Porter (1997). The remaining variance was not attributed to these four effects.

understand.title: Methodological note: what a variance decomposition can and cannot tell you

blocks.text: Variance-decomposition studies answer a descriptive question: across a large sample, how much of the spread in profitability lines up with industry membership, corporate ownership, the year and the individual business? They do not identify causes. The “business-specific” share is partly a residual: it includes good strategy, but also luck, accounting differences and anything else particular to the unit. Industry definitions are borrowed from statistical classification codes that may not match how competitors actually see their market.

Two further cautions matter for executives. First, a share of variance across thousands of businesses is not the importance of industry for *your* decision: in a concentrated service sector structure may dominate, while in a fragmented one execution may. Second, results vary with the sample, period and method, which is why the literature reports a range of estimates rather than a single number. Treat the study as evidence that both levels matter, not as a precise ratio to quote in a board meeting.

challenge.text: The variance results feed a long-running disagreement. Scholars in the positioning tradition point to the sizable, sector-varying industry share as evidence that choosing where to compete is a first-order decision. Scholars in the resource-based tradition (Lesson 3) point to the larger business-specific share as evidence that what happens inside the firm matters more than the industry it enters. Both readings are consistent with the same numbers, because the numbers describe association, not mechanism. The practical conclusion is to analyze both: structure sets the average and the range; the firm determines where it lands within that range.

Several criticisms of the five-forces framework deserve weight. It is largely static: it describes a structure at one moment, while many markets are reshaped by technology faster than any analysis can be updated. It treats buyers and suppliers mainly as threats to bargain against, while many profitable strategies involve cooperation — co-investment with suppliers, joint standards with rivals, platforms that make complementary products more valuable. Brandenburger and Stuart’s framework treats these relationships symmetrically, which makes cooperation as natural a move as competition. And in platform markets, where value depends on how many participants are on each side, the most important question is often whose position in the network is hardest to bypass — a question the five forces address only indirectly.

Industry boundaries are also a choice of the analyst. Is a streaming service competing with other streaming services, with video games, or with sleep? Is a professional sports league competing with other leagues or with every claim on a household’s evening and budget? The answer changes which forces look strong. Porter’s advice — define the industry by the products customers treat as substitutes and the geography within which competition actually occurs — is sound, but applying it requires judgment, and reasonable analysts disagree.

Added value has its own limits. It is a ceiling, not a forecast: a firm with large added value may still capture little if it negotiates poorly or if customers do not perceive the difference. And the numbers it requires — willingness to pay, opportunity costs, the value of the next-best alternative — are rarely observed directly. In practice you estimate them from pricing experiments, lost-deal analysis and the terms on which customers and suppliers walk away. The framework’s value is that it tells you which numbers to look for.

Finally, a frequent misuse: treating the five forces as a form to fill in, rating every force “medium”. The framework earns its keep by identifying the one or two forces that drive profitability in a market and by showing how a firm can position itself where those forces bite least, or reshape them — for example by raising customers’ switching costs or by helping a second supplier emerge.

apply.text: The decisive force is buyer power through **backward integration**: a well-resourced buyer can make the product itself. That reframes the strategic question. The vendor’s added value is not the capture technology as such, which a determined buyer can approximate, but whatever the buyer could not easily reproduce: validated accuracy, an accumulated workflow, time saved for scarce staff and the learning pooled across many clients, where contracts and consent allow it. Pricing above that added value invites the buyer to build its own.

The value-based lens is useful inside player development, where the organization is both a buyer and a supplier. When competing to sign amateur or international players, the relevant question is added value: what does this organization’s development system offer a player that the next-best organization does not? If the honest answer is “nothing distinctive”, the signing will be won on money alone. The same logic applies to hiring coaches and analysts, whose opportunity cost is set by their best alternative employer. Scarce specialists hold supplier power, and a department that ignores it will lose them to whoever recognizes it first.

How would you decide, what would you ask for in return, and what information would change your mind?

lessons.title: Resources, Capabilities and the Build-versus-Buy Decision
lessons.summary: Advantage that lasts usually rests on resources and capabilities rivals cannot buy or copy easily; the theory that says so is hard to use before the fact, and the build-versus-buy decision is where it becomes practical.
objectives: Apply the VRIN criteria — valuable, rare, imperfectly imitable, non-substitutable — to judge whether a resource can sustain an advantage.
Explain dynamic capabilities and why the ability to reconfigure matters when markets change.
Evaluate the tautology critique of the resource-based view and state how to use the framework without falling into it.
Make and defend a build, buy or partner recommendation for a capability.
lessons.executive: Lesson 2 looked outward at industries; this lesson looks inward. The resource-based view holds that sustained advantage comes from resources that are valuable, rare, hard to imitate and hard to substitute — often because they were built through history, depend on many people working together, or are poorly understood even by their owners. Dynamic capabilities extend the idea to the ability to rebuild as markets change. Critics argue the framework is circular unless value is defined by customers and costs rather than by the advantage it explains. Use it to discipline build-versus-buy choices: buy what everyone can buy, and build or protect what will differentiate.

explore.text: Two hospital systems of similar size buy the same clinical-decision software from the same vendor in the same year. Three years later one has cut avoidable readmissions substantially and the other reports no measurable change. The software is identical. The license fee is identical. Whatever explains the difference cannot be the software.
Before reading on: list what might explain the difference. Which of your explanations could the lagging system buy, and which would it have to build?

The likely explanations appear on no invoice: how the tool is woven into nurses’ and physicians’ routines, whether clinicians trust it, whether someone has the authority to act on its alerts, how quickly problems are fixed, whether the data feeding it is clean. Each took time to develop, depends on many people working together, and is hard for an outsider to see, let alone copy. This is the intuition behind the resource-based view of the firm: an advantage that lasts is rarely something you can buy, because anything you can buy, your rival can buy too.

The pattern recurs across fields. Every investment bank can license the same trading platforms, yet their results differ. Every army can buy similar equipment; how units train, coordinate and adapt differs far more. Every sports organization can purchase the same tracking hardware; what it learns from the data and how that learning changes coaching does not come in the box. The question for this lesson is what kinds of resources and capabilities produce advantage that lasts, how you can tell before the fact, and what that implies for the everyday decision of whether to build something or buy it.

understand.text: The resource-based view

Barney’s 1991 article set out the resource-based view (RBV) in the form most often taught. It starts from two assumptions: strategic resources are **heterogeneous** — firms differ in what they control — and **imperfectly mobile**, so those differences can persist because the resources cannot easily be traded or copied. Resources are defined broadly: physical assets, but also organizational processes, information, knowledge, relationships and reputation. Barney proposed that a resource can be a source of *sustained* competitive advantage when it is **valuable** (it helps the firm exploit opportunities or neutralize threats), **rare** among current and potential competitors, **imperfectly imitable**, and without strategically equivalent **substitutes**. Teaching shorthand calls these the VRIN criteria.

The most interesting part concerns imitation. Barney identified three reasons a resource can resist it. **Unique historical conditions**: the resource was acquired or built along a path that cannot be repeated, such as a reputation earned over decades. **Causal ambiguity**: neither the firm nor its rivals fully understand which resources produce the advantage, so rivals do not know what to copy. **Social complexity**: the resource depends on relationships, culture and trust among many people, which cannot be engineered on demand. These are the opposite of what can be purchased.

A hospital’s surgical-team routines refined over years

A software firm’s proprietary training dataset

understand.text: The last row deserves attention. A resource can be valuable and rare and still produce no profit for the organization that holds it, if the resource can bargain for its own value. Highly mobile talent is the classic case: the employee captures the value through pay. This connects the resource-based view to Lesson 2’s logic of value capture. A later teaching version of the framework, often abbreviated VRIO, adds a further question — whether the firm is **organized** to exploit the resource — as a reminder that a valuable asset inside a dysfunctional organization produces nothing.
Capabilities and dynamic capabilities

A **capability** is a repeatable pattern of coordinated activity: the ability to launch a product on schedule, to integrate an acquisition, to recognize and treat sepsis early, to develop junior lawyers into partners. Capabilities live in routines, in the tacit knowledge of experienced people and in the relationships that let them coordinate. They are built by doing, and they decay when unused.

Teece, Pisano and Shuen asked what happens when markets change quickly. They defined **dynamic capabilities** as a firm’s ability to integrate, build and reconfigure internal and external competences to address rapidly changing environments. In their account, advantage depends on a firm’s managerial and organizational **processes** (how it coordinates, learns and reconfigures), its **positions** (its current endowment of technology, assets, customers and relationships) and its **paths** (the strategic alternatives open to it, shaped by its history). Paths matter because capabilities are cumulative: what a firm can learn next depends on what it has already learned.

steps.label: Renewed advantage

blocks.text: Three terms are often used loosely. A **resource** is something the organization controls or can reliably access: equipment, capital, data, a brand, a contract, a skilled person. A **routine** is a recurring pattern of interdependent actions carried out by several people — the way a hospital hands off patients at shift change, or a newsroom checks facts before publication. A **capability** is the reliable ability to perform an activity well, built from resources combined through routines.

The distinction matters for strategy because resources can often be bought, while capabilities usually have to be built. Buying a resource without the routines to use it is like buying a training facility without the coaching program: an asset on the balance sheet, not an advantage in competition.

understand.text: Build, buy or partner

The resource-based view becomes practical in the **build-versus-buy** decision. Buying — contracting with a vendor, licensing, acquiring a finished product — is fast and draws on specialists’ scale. Building internally is slow and expensive but can create something rivals cannot purchase. Partnering — alliances, joint ventures, co-development — sits between them. The core question is not which option is cheaper today but which leaves the organization with an advantage it can defend tomorrow, at an acceptable risk.

y: Capability scarce or immature in the market
Capability widely available in the market

understand.text: Three further questions refine the grid. **Hold-up risk**: if you depend on one vendor for something critical, the vendor gains bargaining power at renewal — Lesson 2’s supplier power. **Learning**: building a capability, even imperfectly, can teach the organization things it cannot learn as a customer, which may matter for the next decision. **Opportunity cost**: the engineers, analysts or clinicians who build one capability are not building another, and in most organizations they are the scarcest resource of all.

blocks.text: Testing the resource-based view is hard for a simple reason: the resources that matter most by the theory’s own logic — tacit, socially complex, causally ambiguous — are the hardest to observe. Empirical studies therefore rely on proxies such as R&D spending, patents, employee tenure or survey ratings of capabilities. Each proxy captures only part of the construct, and some partly reflect performance itself.

Two biases recur. **Reverse causality**: profitable firms can afford to accumulate resources, so a correlation between resources and performance may run from performance to resources. **Survivorship**: firms whose resources failed to create value disappear from samples. A careful reader of resource-based research asks how the resource was measured, whether it was measured before the performance it is said to explain, and whether the comparison includes firms that held similar resources and failed.

challenge.text: In 2001, Priem and Butler argued in the *Academy of Management Review* that the resource-based view, as then formulated, was not yet a theoretical structure. Their central concern was circularity: if a “valuable” resource is defined as one that generates competitive advantage, the claim that valuable resources generate advantage is true by definition. They also argued that the RBV had assumed stable product markets and had not explained how a resource’s value is determined — a value they said is set outside the firm, by demand in product markets. Barney replied in the same issue that the direct criticisms of his framework were unfounded, while accepting that they highlighted requirements for future research. This is a live disagreement about theory construction, not a failed replication: both sides agree resources matter, and they disagree about whether the framework as stated can be falsified.

The practical lesson does not depend on who won the exchange. VRIN is easy to apply after the fact: once a firm has succeeded, it is tempting to label whatever it had as valuable, rare and inimitable. To use the framework before the fact, define value from the outside — which customers will pay more, or which costs will fall, because of this resource, and why will that remain true? Then specify the mechanism that blocks imitation and estimate how long a determined rival would take to close the gap. If you cannot state those, you are describing a hope, not an advantage.

Dynamic capabilities attract a parallel concern. If a dynamic capability is identified by the fact that a firm adapted successfully, the concept explains nothing. APERTURE’s working view is that the idea is most useful when it points to specific, observable processes — how often an organization runs experiments, how quickly it retires old products or programs, how it moves people to new priorities — rather than to an unobservable property inferred from success.

Capabilities can also become traps. The routines that make an organization excellent at one thing make it resistant to another: a newspaper superb at print production, a hospital built around inpatient care, a consulting firm built on large teams of junior analysts. Strengths that once fit the environment can become rigidities that keep the organization from seeing that the environment changed. This is one reason to pair the resource-based view with Lesson 2’s attention to industry structure and Lesson 4’s attention to uncertainty.

Finally, “build” is often romanticized. Internal teams underestimate maintenance, security and documentation; a capability built by two talented people can vanish when they leave; and organizations frequently build what they could have bought because building is more interesting to the builders. A credible build case states who will maintain the capability in three years and what it will cost.

A mid-sized hospital system is deciding how to obtain an early-warning model for sepsis. A vendor offers a validated model integrated with the hospital’s record system for a license fee. An internal data-science team argues it could build a model tuned to the system’s own patients. A university research group proposes to co-develop and publish one. The figures below are synthetic.

apply.text: The heuristic points to a split decision. The prediction model itself is increasingly available in the market, so buying it is defensible. But the opening example suggests the advantage lies in how alerts are acted upon — escalation routines, nurses’ authority to act, response times. That is not for sale. A reasonable recommendation is to buy the model on terms that guarantee data access and local performance reporting, and to invest the internal team’s time in the clinical workflow and in monitoring how the model performs on the system’s own patients. The option to build later is preserved, because the team learns the data in the meantime. A defensible alternative would be to partner, if the system values publication and the learning it brings more than speed.

Player development faces the same choice with tracking systems, biomechanics tools and analytics platforms. Hardware and standard software are widely available, so buying is usually sound; any rival can buy the same equipment. What rivals cannot purchase is the routine that turns measurement into better coaching — how data reaches coaches, whether players trust it, how quickly the organization tests and retires drills, and its accumulated, organization-specific record of what worked for whom. Those are the resources the VRIN test favors, and they are built through people and process, not procurement. Data-rights terms in vendor contracts matter for the same reason: they decide whether the organization can build on its own data later.

retain.text: Sustained advantage rarely comes from what can be bought. The resource-based view points to resources that are valuable, rare, hard to imitate and hard to substitute, often because of history, social complexity or causal ambiguity; dynamic capabilities stress the ability to rebuild as markets change. The framework becomes circular if value is defined by success, so define value from customers and costs, and use it to decide what to buy, what to build and what to protect.

lessons.title: Advantage Under Competition and Uncertainty
lessons.summary: Edges built on information get competed away; durable strategy under uncertainty combines a few hard-to-reverse commitments with staged options, and is revealed by what the organization actually funds.
objectives: Interpret evidence on how a mispriced skill in a professional sports labor market was priced away, and generalize the mechanism to other industries.
Use real-options reasoning and scenarios to decide when to commit and when to stage an investment.
Distinguish intended from realized strategy and diagnose an allocation that contradicts its stated strategy.
lessons.executive: An advantage that rests on knowing something rivals do not is temporary by design: once visible, it is imitated and priced away. Hakes and Sauer found that pattern in baseball’s labor market — on-base skill was underpriced, and the gap narrowed after the idea became public. When everyone has the same data, the edge moves to what is slow to copy: speed, integration, adoption and proprietary learning. Under uncertainty, commit firmly to the few choices that are costly to reverse and stage the rest as options. Then audit your budget, because the strategy you actually have is the one you fund.

explore.text: In 2003, a best-selling book by Michael Lewis described how a low-payroll professional baseball club competed with far richer rivals by buying skills that the market underpriced — most famously, the ability of hitters to get on base. The story became a parable far beyond sport: find the measure others ignore, buy it cheaply, win. It also raised a question economists could test. If the market really was underpricing a skill, what should happen once the idea was published?

Before reading on: predict what happened to the salary premium for on-base skill in the seasons after the book appeared. Then predict how long the advantage of the first organizations to exploit it should have lasted.

Every industry has its version of the parable. A quantitative fund discovers a pricing anomaly. A retailer learns before its rivals that a neighborhood is about to change. A hospital finds that an inexpensive intervention reduces readmissions. A consulting firm develops a diagnostic tool that clients love. Each is an edge built on knowing something others do not. This lesson asks three questions: what happens to such edges, what kinds of advantage survive when everyone has analytics, and how should an organization commit resources when the future is genuinely uncertain? The last question brings the week back to its starting point, because the answer is written not in plans but in budgets.

understand.text: Evidence: pricing away an edge

Hakes and Sauer tested the book’s claim with standard econometric methods on major-league data from 1999 to 2004. They estimated how much a team’s on-base percentage and its slugging percentage each contributed to winning, and how much the salary market paid players for each skill. Their results supported the central claim: before the book’s publication, on-base skill was undervalued in the labor market relative to its contribution to winning. They also found that the undervaluation diminished after the book was published, as salaries came to reflect the skill more fully.

The finding matters less for baseball history than for strategy. The edge was real, measurable and valuable — and it was temporary. Once a mispricing is visible, competitors bid for the underpriced asset, its price rises toward its value, and the advantage passes to whoever finds the next mispricing. The same mechanism is familiar in finance, where a widely publicized pricing anomaly attracts capital until it shrinks. In the language of Lesson 3, an insight that becomes public stops being rare.

steps.label: Mispricing exists
steps.text: An input is valued below its contribution

steps.label: Early exploitation
steps.text: A few organizations buy it cheaply

steps.label: Visibility
steps.text: Results, hires or publications reveal the idea

steps.label: Imitation
steps.text: Rivals bid for the same input

steps.label: Price correction
steps.text: The input’s price rises toward its value

steps.label: Edge moves
steps.text: Advantage shifts to the next insight or to execution

understand.title: Methodological note: how strong is the evidence that the edge was competed away?

blocks.text: Hakes and Sauer’s design is observational. It compares estimated salary returns to a skill across seasons and interprets the change after publication as a market response. That is persuasive but not proof. Other things changed in the same years; the window after publication in their data is short; and salary regressions depend on which player characteristics are controlled for. Publication of the book is also not the only possible channel: the same ideas were already circulating inside the industry.

The paper drew public debate, including the argument that the featured club’s success owed more to its pitching than to on-base skill. On the replication side, a later undergraduate honors thesis reported reproducing the main regressions and cross-validating them with a simulation model. A fair summary is that the evidence consistently points to an initial mispricing that narrowed, while the precise timing and cause of the correction are less certain than popular retellings suggest.

understand.text: When everyone has analytics

If information edges erode, what is left when every competitor has similar data, similar models and similar analysts? APERTURE’s working hypothesis, drawn from the resource-based logic of Lesson 3 rather than from a specific study, is that advantage migrates to things that are slow to copy: the speed with which insight becomes action; how well analysis is integrated into the decisions of the people who do the work; trust between analysts and practitioners; the organization’s ability to generate proprietary data through its own experiments; and its capacity to keep the people who hold this knowledge. These are socially complex and causally ambiguous — the attributes Barney identified.

The hypothesis has a counterintuitive implication. The more widely a tool is available, the less buying it differentiates, and the more the complementary investments around it matter. Organizations that treat analytics as a purchase compete on parity; those that treat it as a capability compete on adoption, integration and learning. It also implies a competitive response problem: rivals watch what you do. A visible edge invites imitation, so the durable question is not “what do we know?” but “what will we still know, or be able to do, after they have copied it?”
Committing under uncertainty: options and scenarios

Strategic commitments are often irreversible: a facility, an acquisition, a market entry, a long contract. Under uncertainty, irreversibility gives flexibility a value. **Real-options reasoning**, borrowed from finance, treats some strategic investments as the right but not the obligation to act later — to expand if a pilot succeeds, to abandon if it fails, to wait until uncertainty resolves. The intuition is simple: when you can cut off the downside, uncertainty raises the value of the opportunity. A pilot is valuable not for its own returns but because it buys information before the large commitment.

A synthetic example shows the arithmetic. A company can commit $10 million now to a new service. With probability 0.5 the market is strong and the investment returns $18 million; with probability 0.5 it is weak and returns $4 million. The expected value of committing now is 0.5 × 18 + 0.5 × 4 − 10 = $1 million. Alternatively, it can spend $1 million on a pilot that reveals the state of the market, then invest $10 million only if the market is strong. The expected value is 0.5 × (18 − 10) − 1 = $3 million, assuming the pilot delays nothing that matters. Staging is worth more because it avoids the $6 million loss in the weak state. The comparison reverses if waiting lets a rival take the market first — the reason options thinking never removes the need for judgment.

understand.title: Prerequisite: expected value and the value of information

blocks.text: The **expected value** of an uncertain choice is the probability-weighted average of its outcomes. It is a guide for repeated or portfolio decisions, not a promise about any single outcome, and it ignores tolerance for risk: a choice with a higher expected value but a small chance of ruin may still be unwise.

The **value of information** is the improvement in expected value from learning something before deciding. Information is worth paying for only if it could change the decision. A study whose result would not alter what you do is worth nothing, however interesting. That principle disciplines both pilots and requests for more analysis.

understand.text: **Scenario planning** is a practitioner method for strategy under deep uncertainty, presented here as a heuristic rather than a validated technique. Instead of forecasting one future, a team identifies the two or three uncertainties that most affect its strategy and constructs a small set of plausible, internally consistent futures that differ on them. The strategy is then tested for robustness: which commitments pay off in every scenario (no-regret moves), which pay off only in some (options to stage), and which would be disastrous in at least one (risks to hedge). Rigorous evidence that scenario planning improves organizational performance is thin; its plausible benefit is that it counters overconfidence in a single forecast.

understand.caption: Commit, stage, experiment or avoid
cells: Avoid, or hold as a small staged option until uncertainty resolves
Commit deliberately: this is a core strategic bet
Experiment cheaply; stop quickly if the signal is weak
understand.note: APERTURE heuristic for sorting initiatives across scenarios; not a validated model.

understand.text: Realized strategy is what you fund

Mintzberg and Waters’ distinction between intended and realized strategy has a direct financial meaning. An organization’s realized strategy is visible in its stream of actions, and few actions reveal it more clearly than resource commitments: which projects are funded, which people are moved, which requests are refused. When the stated strategy says “focus” but the budget gives every unit a small increase, the realized strategy is the budget.

Executives call the result **peanut-butter allocation**: spreading resources thinly and evenly across every initiative to avoid conflict. It feels fair and is politically safe. It is usually incoherent. Under diminishing returns, a little money for everything can be defensible when initiatives are equally important — but a strategy makes initiatives unequal by design, and many initiatives have a minimum scale below which they produce little. An emergency department funded at 60% of what it needs is not 60% of an emergency department.

challenge.text: Real-options reasoning has its own failure mode: it can rationalize never committing. An organization that treats every strategic move as a small pilot may never build anything at the scale needed to matter, and rivals who commit early can take the best customers, locations or talent. Commitment also has strategic value of its own. An irreversible investment signals to rivals and partners that you will not retreat, which can deter entry or attract partners. The disciplined position is to stage what is uncertain and reversible, and to commit deliberately to the few things that define the position.

Scenario planning can become an elaborate exercise that changes nothing if no decision is attached to it, or a way to avoid choosing by preparing for everything at once. Its outputs are only as good as the uncertainties chosen, and groups tend to select the uncertainties they already worry about. A useful test: if the scenarios did not change at least one allocation, they were decoration.

The erosion story has limits too. Not every edge is competed away quickly. Some advantages rest on assets that cannot be bid away — a location, a regulatory license, a network that becomes more valuable as it grows — and some organizations keep finding the next edge because their real capability is the search itself. The point is not that lasting advantage is impossible, but that advantages built on information alone should be expected to decay, and planned for accordingly.

Finally, the allocation lens can be misused. A budget that concentrates resources is not automatically strategic; it may simply reflect who argued loudest. Concentration is a virtue only when it follows from a diagnosis and a guiding policy. The same budget can be coherent under one strategy and incoherent under another — which is exactly what this week’s exercise asks you to explore.

apply.text: Worked example: two budgets, one strategy

A state public-health department adopts a strategy to reduce opioid overdose deaths, with a guiding policy of concentrating on the highest-risk moment: the weeks after release from jail or discharge from hospital. Its $20 million budget (synthetic) is then assembled through the usual process, in which each program defends its share.

apply.caption: Stated strategy versus realized allocation (synthetic)
rows: Naloxone distribution at release and discharge
Peer navigators for the first 30 days
Grants to every county health office

apply.text: The proposed budget is not wrong line by line: every program has supporters and some rationale. It is wrong as a whole, because it puts only about a third of the money into the activities the guiding policy says matter most. Realigning it does not abolish the other programs; it admits that the strategy is a choice. The realigned budget also tells everyone what will be done less — the media campaign and the county grants — which is where the political work lies, and where a leader’s credibility is spent.

Professional baseball offers a vivid version of this lesson. Analytical methods in player evaluation and development that were once rare are now widely shared across organizations, much as the labor-market evidence on on-base skill showed for an earlier generation of ideas. If the edge from having data is shrinking, the questions for a development leader shift: how quickly does insight change what coaches do on a given afternoon; how well does the organization learn from its own interventions; how does it keep the staff who carry that knowledge; and what will it stop funding in order to concentrate on those? A department that answers by giving every program a small increase has chosen a strategy, whether or not it meant to.

apply.title: Executive twist: the edge just became public

blocks.text: An analyst who used to work for a rival presents your organization’s signature method at a public conference — not your data, but the idea. Some of your staff believe the edge is gone; your leadership asks whether to keep investing. You do not know how quickly rivals can implement the method, or whether your advantage was ever the idea rather than the way your people use it. What evidence would you gather in the next 30 days, what commitments would you pause, and what would you double down on?

retain.text: Information-based edges are temporary: once visible, they are imitated and priced away, as the evidence on on-base skill suggests. When tools are widely available, advantage migrates to integration, adoption, speed and proprietary learning. Under uncertainty, commit deliberately to the few hard-to-reverse choices, stage the rest as options and test robustness across scenarios. Then check the budget: realized strategy is what you fund.
Explain, without notes, why an edge based on information tends to erode, and name one kind of advantage that erodes more slowly.
In the staged-investment example, why is the pilot worth more than its own returns?
Look at the last budget you influenced. What strategy does it reveal, and is it the one you intended?

takeaways: Edges built on information are temporary: visibility invites imitation and prices the edge away.
When everyone has similar tools, advantage shifts to integration, adoption, speed and proprietary learning.
Real options give flexibility a value: stage uncertain, reversible moves; commit deliberately to the few that define the position.
Scenarios test robustness — no-regret moves, options and hedges — but only matter if they change an allocation.
Realized strategy is visible in resource allocation; peanut-butter spreading is a strategy of avoiding choice.

check.prompt: Which interpretation of this fictional finding is most consistent with this lesson?

stimulus.text: Fictional study. In a regional freight-brokerage market, three early adopters of a data-driven pricing method earned operating margins about 4 percentage points above the market average in 2019–2020. A trade-press article described the method in 2021. By 2023, twenty brokers used similar methods, and the early adopters’ margin advantage had fallen to about 0.5 points, although the method’s forecasting accuracy had not declined.

options.text: The method never worked; the early advantage was luck.
The edge was information-based; as imitation spread, competition passed the gains to customers and the advantage eroded.
The early adopters must have executed the method worse after 2021.
The article caused a fall in market demand for freight brokerage.

check.explanation: The method kept working — its accuracy did not decline — but its advantage shrank as twenty rivals adopted similar methods after it became visible. That is the life cycle of an information-based edge: visibility, imitation, correction. The remaining advantage, if any, would have to come from execution, proprietary data or speed.

optionFeedback.a: Luck cannot be ruled out from one market, but the timing of the decline after the article and wide adoption points to imitation, and the method’s accuracy held up.
optionFeedback.c: Nothing in the finding suggests worse execution; the advantage fell because rivals caught up.
optionFeedback.d: The finding concerns margins relative to the market average, so a market-wide fall in demand would not explain a shrinking relative advantage.

check.prompt: A firm can commit $8M now to a new product. With probability 0.4 demand is strong and the product is worth $20M; otherwise it is worth $5M. Alternatively, a $0.5M pilot would reveal demand, after which the firm would invest the $8M only if demand is strong. Assuming the pilot delays nothing that matters, what is the expected value of the staged approach, in $M?
check.working: Staged: 0.4 × (20 − 8) − 0.5 = 4.8 − 0.5 = 4.3. For comparison, committing now: 0.4 × 20 + 0.6 × 5 − 8 = 8 + 3 − 8 = 3.0. Staging adds 1.3 because it avoids the 8 − 5 = 3 loss in the weak state (probability 0.6, worth 1.8) at a cost of 0.5.
check.explanation: The pilot is worth paying for because its result changes the decision: in the weak state the firm does not invest. The value of staging comes from cutting off the downside, not from the pilot’s own returns. If waiting allowed a rival to take the market first, the comparison could reverse.
