glossary.definition: Performing similar activities better than rivals — faster, cheaper, with fewer errors. Necessary for superior performance but, in Porter’s account, not sufficient, because the practices diffuse.
Performing different activities from rivals, or similar activities in different ways, to deliver a distinctive mix of value to a chosen set of customers.
A strategic choice in which more of one thing means less of another, so that activities suited to one position are unsuited to another. Trade-offs make positions hard to copy.
Trying to occupy two incompatible positions at once, which carries the costs of both and the advantages of neither.
The degree to which an organization’s activities are consistent with its strategy and reinforce one another. Fit protects a position because rivals must copy a system, not a single practice.
Rumelt’s core of a good strategy: a diagnosis of the critical challenge, a guiding policy for dealing with it, and coherent actions that carry the policy out.
The value of the best alternative given up by making a choice. Every allocation of money, people or attention has one.
Porter’s framework for industry profitability: threat of entry, supplier power, buyer power, threat of substitutes and rivalry among competitors.
The most a customer would pay for a product rather than go without it. The top of the value line; value created is willingness to pay minus suppliers’ opportunity cost.
The total value created with a particular player minus the total value created without it. Brandenburger and Stuart show that a firm cannot capture more than its added value.
The theory that sustained competitive advantage comes from resources and capabilities that differ across firms and cannot easily be traded or copied.
Barney’s criteria for a resource that can sustain advantage: valuable, rare, imperfectly imitable and non-substitutable.
Uncertainty, even inside the firm, about which resources produce an advantage, which leaves rivals unsure what to copy.
A firm’s ability to integrate, build and reconfigure internal and external competences in response to rapidly changing environments (Teece, Pisano and Shuen).
A strategic investment treated as the right but not the obligation to act later — to expand, stage, wait or abandon — which gives flexibility value under uncertainty.
A practitioner method that tests a strategy against a few plausible, internally consistent futures rather than a single forecast, to find no-regret moves, options and risks.
A pattern in an organization’s actions that was realized without having been intended (Mintzberg and Waters); contrasted with deliberate strategy.
Executive slang for spreading resources thinly and evenly across all initiatives to avoid conflict, which usually contradicts any stated strategy.

exercise.title: Strategy Table

intro.text: You sit at the leadership table of **Quarrow Animal Health**, a fictional regional group of 38 general-practice veterinary clinics. The board has approved a three-year investment budget of $10 million — 100 points of $100,000 each — and asked the team to choose one strategic posture and allocate the budget to match it. Eight initiatives compete for the money. Three scenarios describe how the next three years might unfold.

items: Choose a posture. Read all three before you choose; each is a coherent strategy.
Allocate the 100 points in steps of 5. You do not have to fund every initiative, and no initiative can exceed its maximum.
Inspect the value of your allocation in each scenario, its concentration (Herfindahl index) and the rules that fire.
Then run three experiments: (1) keep your allocation but switch posture; (2) spread the budget evenly, 10–15 points each; (3) put at least 45 points on a single initiative. Note what changes and why.
Finally, list the initiatives you would fund in every scenario (no-regret moves) and those you would stage until the uncertainty resolves.

intro.text: What to notice: whether your allocation expresses the posture you chose; how much value an incoherent allocation gives up; which initiatives are robust across scenarios and which are bets on one future. Keep a clear line between the model’s **illustrative assumptions** (every number in it) and the **empirical claims** from this week’s readings (for example, that diminishing returns and opportunity costs are real, or that information-based edges erode). The model illustrates the logic; it does not measure anything.

brief.text: Quarrow Animal Health (fictional) runs 38 general-practice clinics across a three-state region. Revenue has grown with pet ownership, but margins are under pressure: veterinarians and technicians are scarce and expensive, independent clinics compete on relationships, and a national consolidator has begun buying practices in neighboring states. Pet owners increasingly drive long distances at night or for complex procedures because the region lacks specialty and emergency capacity.

The leadership team agrees on the facts and disagrees on the strategy. The medical director wants Quarrow to become the region’s destination for complex care. The chief operating officer wants a lower-cost, more convenient network for routine care. The chief financial officer sees an opportunity to sell software, lab work and specialty referrals to the region’s independent clinics. The board will fund one posture coherently; it has said it will not fund three half-strategies.

brief.caption: Quarrow at a glance (synthetic)
rows: Share of clients who left the region for emergency or specialty care last year
brief.note: Synthetic data for a fictional organization.

strategies.label: Specialty destination
strategies.description: Differentiate on advanced care: become the region’s referral destination for complex and emergency cases, with the general clinics as the front door.

strategies.label: Everyday value network
strategies.description: Compete on convenience and cost for routine care: standardized, accessible, subscription-based and efficient.

strategies.label: Partner platform
strategies.description: Become the supplier and referral partner of the region’s independent clinics — software, laboratory services and specialty referrals — while keeping the clinic network.

initiatives.label: Specialty referral hospital
initiatives.description: A regional hospital for surgery, oncology, cardiology and advanced imaging, taking referrals from Quarrow clinics and independents.
initiatives.notes: Needs roughly 30 points or more to open at a viable size; depends on recruiting board-certified specialists, who are scarce. Highest upside, slowest payback.

initiatives.label: 24-hour emergency and critical care
initiatives.description: Two overnight emergency sites covering the region.
initiatives.notes: Staffing-heavy and expensive per case; fills a real gap for clients at night; feeds specialty referrals.

initiatives.label: Telehealth triage and wellness subscriptions
initiatives.description: A remote triage line plus monthly plans bundling routine visits, vaccines and dental care.
initiatives.notes: Smooths demand and raises client retention; depends on clinician time to answer calls.

initiatives.label: Shared services and procurement
initiatives.description: Central purchasing, scheduling, billing and inventory for all clinics.
initiatives.notes: Lowers cost per visit and pays back quickly; clients barely notice it.

initiatives.label: Clinician recruiting, retention and training
initiatives.description: Scholarships, technician career ladders, mentoring and flexible schedules.
initiatives.notes: Almost every other initiative depends on clinicians; value rises sharply if shortages deepen.

initiatives.label: Software and lab services for independent clinics
initiatives.description: Practice-management software, a diagnostic laboratory and a referral network sold to independent practices.
initiatives.notes: A different business with different customers and sales skills; large upside if independents stay independent.

initiatives.label: Regional brand campaign
initiatives.description: Advertising and community sponsorships across the region.
initiatives.notes: Raises awareness quickly; easily matched by rivals.

initiatives.label: Data and analytics
initiatives.description: An outcomes registry, demand forecasting and pricing analysis across clinics.
initiatives.notes: Small and broadly useful; most valuable when tied to specific decisions.

scenarios.label: Base case
scenarios.description: Demand grows modestly; clinician supply stays tight but stable.

scenarios.label: Clinician shortage deepens
scenarios.description: Wages rise and specialists are scarce: staffing-heavy initiatives lose value; recruiting and remote care gain.

scenarios.label: A national consolidator enters on price
scenarios.description: The consolidator buys independents and undercuts routine-care prices: efficiency and differentiation gain; selling to independents loses.

rules.text: Every initiative has at least 10 points. Under a specialty-destination posture this is peanut-butter allocation: the referral hospital and emergency care — the activities that define the position — are held below the scale at which they work, while initiatives the posture barely values still absorb money. For each 10-point slice, ask what it is for.

Every initiative has at least 10 points. An everyday-value posture does fund many small, reinforcing activities, so spreading costs less here than under the other postures — but money in the specialty hospital and the software business works against a low-cost, convenient position. Coherence is about where the money goes, not only how concentrated it is.

Every initiative has at least 10 points. A partner-platform posture lives or dies on the offer to independent clinics; spreading the budget leaves that offer underbuilt while consumer-facing initiatives compete with the very partners you want.

You are building a software and laboratory business for independent clinics under a specialty-destination posture. Independents are a referral source for a specialty hospital, so some support may fit — but a software business has different customers, sales skills and capabilities, and at this scale it competes for management attention with the hospital build. Is this a hedge, or straddling?

Subscription plans and telehealth triage are the core of an everyday-value position. Funding them heavily inside a specialty posture risks straddling: two operating models and two promises to clients, run by one leadership team.

Nearly half the budget is on one high-risk asset. Check the clinician-shortage scenario: the referral hospital loses 40% of its value if specialists cannot be hired. If you keep this bet, fund recruiting and retention alongside it — a specialty hospital without specialists is a building.

Coherent pairing: the referral hospital is funded at a workable scale and the clinician program supplies the specialists and technicians it depends on. This is the kind of fit between activities that an additive model understates.

A specialty referral hospital inside an everyday-value network is the classic straddle: a premium cost structure and brand attached to a strategy built on convenience and price. Unless it serves a clear referral need of your own clinics, this money works against the posture.

Coherent core: telehealth triage, subscription plans and shared services reinforce each other — lower cost per visit, more predictable demand, more capacity per clinician. Check that clinician recruiting is funded too; convenience fails without staff.

Round-the-clock emergency care is staffing-heavy and costly per case. Under an everyday-value posture, consider whether a partnership with an existing emergency hospital would serve your clients at lower cost, freeing points for the core.

A consumer brand campaign under a partner-platform posture sends a mixed message: independent clinics are asked to trust you as a supplier while you advertise against them to pet owners. Who is your customer?

This is a real platform bet. Two cautions the numbers do not show: you still own 38 clinics that compete with the independents you want as customers (channel conflict), and if the consolidator buys many independents, this initiative loses 40% of its value. What would make partners trust you — and what would you give up to earn it?

key.insights: What a careful analyst notices. (1) Under every posture, the best allocations in this model concentrate most of the budget on the three or four initiatives the posture values, but coherence is not the same as concentration: the everyday-value posture’s best allocation is fairly broad (Herfindahl index about 0.17) because its fitting initiatives are many and small, while the specialty posture’s is more concentrated (about 0.25). (2) An even spread of 10–15 points per initiative gives up roughly 5–20% of value against the best allocation for the same posture in the base case, and up to about a quarter in the consolidator scenario under the specialty posture. (3) An allocation built for one posture loses roughly a fifth to a third of its value when judged under another — strategy–allocation mismatch costs more than spreading. (4) Clinician recruiting and retention earns 10–25 points in the best allocation for every posture and scenario: it is the no-regret move, because almost every other initiative depends on it. (5) Under the specialty posture, the referral hospital contributes the most value of any initiative in the base and consolidator scenarios and loses the most in the shortage scenario, where the best allocation moves points from it to recruiting — the posture’s defining bet is also its main exposure. (6) The platform posture’s central initiative is the one most damaged by consolidation, and the model cannot see the channel conflict of owning clinics that compete with your customers. (7) Because the model is additive and has no minimum scales, it understates both the cost of spreading and the value of fit; the rules carry those points in words. These figures come from the stated assumptions, not from data.

debrief.text: The Strategy Table makes three ideas from this week visible. First, **coherence beats spreading**: an allocation that funds the activities a posture depends on outperforms one that gives every initiative something, even in a model with diminishing returns built in. Second, **mismatch is expensive**: the same allocation can be strong under one strategy and weak under another, which is why a budget must be read against the strategy it claims to serve. Third, **robustness differs across initiatives**: some commitments pay off in every scenario, others are bets on one future, and a leader should know which is which before committing.

The underlying ideas have different evidential status. That resources have opportunity costs and that marginal returns usually diminish are core economic reasoning. That realized strategy shows up in resource commitments follows Mintzberg and Waters’ distinction between intended and realized strategy. That positions require trade-offs and fit follows Porter’s argument. These are concepts and arguments, not measurements of veterinary markets.

What the exercise does **not** show. Every number in it — the posture weights, the scales, the saturation points, the scenario multipliers — is an illustrative assumption chosen by the case author. The model is additive, so it ignores complementarities between initiatives (Porter’s fit), minimum scales below which an initiative produces nothing, competitors’ responses, execution capacity and the time it takes to build a capability. It cannot see channel conflict, culture or the politics of telling a department that its budget will shrink. Treat its outputs as a structured argument about fit and robustness, not as a forecast.

The same structure applies to a player-development budget. Initiatives such as coaching staff, technology, research, international facilities, education programs and medical support can each be valuable, and a posture — for example, concentrating on a few high-leverage development stages, or on breadth across a large system — changes which ones matter most. Spreading increases evenly across all of them is a strategy too, and rarely the one leaders say they have.

assumptions: Quarrow Animal Health, its figures and its scenarios are fictional; all numbers are synthetic.
Value of an initiative = posture weight × scale × (1 − e^(−points ÷ saturation)) × scenario multiplier. Diminishing returns are a modelling assumption, not an estimate.
Posture weights (0.3–1.5) are the case author’s judgments of strategic fit, not empirical estimates.
Values are comparable across allocations within one posture. Comparing totals across postures is not meaningful, because each posture weights initiatives differently.
The model is additive: it ignores complementarities among initiatives, minimum viable scale, competitors’ responses and execution risk. Rules flag some of these in words.
Risk labels (low, medium, high) are qualitative descriptions and do not enter the calculation.
Concentration is the Herfindahl index of budget shares: 0.125 is a perfectly even spread across eight initiatives; 1.0 puts everything in one.

case.title: Ferrovane Labs: Deeper, Broader or Underneath?
case.fiction: All people, organizations and data in this case are fictional. Any resemblance to real companies or people is coincidental.

body.text: At 6:40 on a Tuesday morning, Nadia Okonkwo-Reyes read the email from her lead investor for the third time. It was two sentences long. “The board needs a strategy, not a menu. Six weeks.” She closed the laptop, opened it again, and began a list of everything she did not know.

Okonkwo-Reyes had founded Ferrovane Labs seven years earlier with Tomas Lindqvist, a computer-vision engineer she had met while working in a university motion laboratory. Their insight was that the expensive marker-based motion capture used in research laboratories — reflective dots on the body, a dozen cameras, hours of processing — could be replaced by ordinary high-speed cameras and software that estimated the position of every joint directly from video. Their product, Ferrovane Studio, combined camera arrays installed in a client’s facility with software that turned movement into joint angles, timing and estimated loads, and with dashboards for coaches, sports scientists and medical staff. A team of “performance engineers” travelled to clients to configure systems and help staff interpret the data.

The early years had gone better than the founders had hoped. Ferrovane now served 64 organizations: professional clubs in soccer, basketball, American football and baseball in North America and Europe, 22 university athletic departments and two military human-performance laboratories. Annual recurring revenue had reached $30.4 million, and the company employed 140 people. Clients paid on average a little under half a million dollars a year, renewed annually.

The trouble was in the trend. Revenue growth had slowed from 60% to 38% to 21% over the last three years. The company had signed 22 new clients in the second of those years and only 11 in the most recent one. Net revenue retention — how much revenue existing clients generated a year later, including upgrades and downgrades — had slipped from 121% to 109%. More worrying to Okonkwo-Reyes was a pattern hidden inside that number. Three of the largest clients had hired their own biomechanists and engineers and now licensed only Ferrovane’s raw capture, at roughly a third of the full price, doing the analysis themselves. “They learned from us,” the head of customer success had said, “and then they didn’t need us.”

Eight months earlier, a dominant smartphone platform company had released a free toolkit that let any developer estimate body pose from a single phone camera. Within months a dozen consumer apps offered “biomechanics” for golfers, runners and youth pitchers. Ferrovane’s internal benchmark showed its multi-camera system was far more accurate for fast, explosive movements such as sprinting and throwing, and only modestly better for slow movements such as walking and squatting. But the benchmark had been run by Ferrovane, and the platform company improved its toolkit every year.

The company had $24 million in the bank and was losing about $1 million a month. That gave it roughly two years — less if it spent heavily. The lead investor, whose fund had put in most of the company’s capital, wanted a credible path to $100 million in annual revenue within five years, or a sale.
Three of Okonkwo-Reyes’s executives had each brought her a strategy. Each was intelligent, and each was incompatible with the other two.

**Go deeper.** Priya Raman, the chief revenue officer, wanted Ferrovane to become the operating system for elite performance departments. That meant integrating with the athlete-management systems clubs already used, adding validated injury-risk models built with research partners, moving clients to three-year contracts and raising prices by 15%. It would cost about $12 million over two years, much of it in engineering and research validation. “Our customers pay us half a million dollars a year,” she said. “The phone toolkit cannot do what we do on a sprint or a throw. We should be the system they cannot rip out.” Her own estimate was that about 900 organizations worldwide could pay more than $250,000 a year for such a system. Ferrovane had 64 of them. A pricing test supported her: six clients offered an integration bundle at 15% more, and four accepted. One declined. The sixth said it was building its own.

**Go broad.** Okonkwo-Reyes herself had long believed that elite sport was a beachhead, not a destination. A consumer app, Ferrovane Form, used a phone camera and a simplified version of the company’s models to give youth, amateur and recreational athletes feedback on their movement for $14.99 a month. A pilot had produced 4,800 downloads and 1,900 paid trials, and 34% of trial users were still paying after eight weeks. The cost of acquiring a user through paid social media had been $62. Scaling the app would cost about $15 million over two years, mostly in marketing and a consumer product team. “Every athlete deserves to see how they move,” she had written in the company’s first pitch deck. She still believed it. She also knew that most of the pilot’s users had come through clients’ youth academies, not through paid advertising, and that Ferrovane had never marketed anything to consumers.

**Go underneath.** Lindqvist argued that the company’s real asset was its engine, not its dashboards. He wanted to license the capture-and-analysis engine as an interface that other software companies could build on: a physical-therapy telehealth platform, a broadcaster’s graphics supplier and a workplace-safety insurer were already paying between $40,000 and $90,000 a year each in a pilot, and fourteen more were in conversation. Rebuilding the engine for that purpose would cost about $8 million. “Let other people fight over customers,” he said. “We should be in every product, and in none of them.” Only one of the three pilot partners had renewed so far. The insurer wanted exclusivity in its category and access to aggregated movement data. Ferrovane’s elite contracts prohibited using clients’ athlete data to train models for third parties, and the company’s general counsel had warned that consent for any secondary use of athletes’ data would need careful review.

The chief financial officer, Gideon Achterberg, had not brought a strategy. He had brought a spreadsheet. “We can afford one big bet,” he told the executive team, “maybe one and a half. If we fund the consumer app at the level Nadia wants, our runway falls to about fourteen months. If we try all three, we will run out of money before any of them works.”

Then, two weeks ago, the situation changed again. Marlowe Tate Group, a large sporting-goods and sports-media company, approached Okonkwo-Reyes with two alternatives. It would acquire Ferrovane outright for about $140 million, a price that would return roughly three times the investors’ capital. Or it would invest $20 million for a minority stake, in exchange for exclusive rights to use Ferrovane’s technology in team-sport broadcasting and in consumer products. The lead investor was clearly tempted. Lindqvist read the offer as proof that the engine was worth far more. Raman read it differently: several elite clients negotiated media rights with Marlowe Tate’s broadcast partners, and she doubted they would share sensitive athlete data with a company partly owned by a media group. Neither offer was binding, and Marlowe Tate had asked for an answer within sixty days.

Okonkwo-Reyes looked again at her list of unknowns. Was the accuracy gap durable, or would the free toolkit close it within two years? Would elite clients pay for deeper integration, or would more of them build their own teams once they had learned enough? Did the consumer pilot measure demand, or the enthusiasm of academy families who already knew the brand? Would the engine still be worth licensing if the platform company’s toolkit kept improving? And what did her 140 employees, most of whom had joined to work with elite athletes, believe the company was for?
She opened a new document and typed the board memo’s first heading: *Diagnosis*. Then she stopped. Pick one path, she thought, and we might be wrong. Pick all three, and we will certainly be wrong.

assumptions: All figures are synthetic and simplified; taxes, debt and option dilution are ignored.

questions: What is your diagnosis of Ferrovane’s critical challenge — slowing growth, commoditization, buyer power, or something else — and which evidence in the case supports it?
Using the five forces and added value, where does Ferrovane’s defensible added value lie today, and how would each option change it?
Which of Ferrovane’s resources pass the VRIN test, and which only look valuable because the company has been successful so far?
Design a sequence: what would you commit to now, what would you stage as an option, what would you stop, and which leading indicators would trigger expanding or ending each?
Under what conditions is selling the company, or accepting the strategic investment, the best strategy? What would you have to believe?

perspectives.title: Go deeper: become the system elite clients cannot remove
perspectives.text: Ferrovane’s added value is greatest where accuracy on explosive movement matters and where integration with clients’ workflows is costly to rebuild. Deepening that position raises switching costs and turns the threat of in-house substitution into a reason to buy more. The pricing test is encouraging. The weaknesses are a hard ceiling on the market, continued buyer power from the largest clients, and the risk that the accuracy gap narrows; this path also asks employees to accept that the company will be smaller and more focused than the founders imagined.

perspectives.title: Go broad: the mission and the market are elsewhere
perspectives.text: Elite sport is a small market whose biggest buyers are learning to build their own systems. If pose estimation is commoditizing, the scarce assets are brand, trusted content and a relationship with millions of athletes, and the time to build them is before rivals do. The pilot’s retention is respectable for a paid app. The case against is strong: the pilot sample is biased toward existing fans, Ferrovane has no consumer capability, the core technology is now free, and this path consumes most of the runway before the evidence arrives.

perspectives.title: Go underneath: the engine is the asset
perspectives.text: Licensing the engine plays to Ferrovane’s most distinctive resource and lets partners bear the cost of reaching customers. It is the cheapest option and keeps the elite business intact. Its risks are that free toolkits erode the engine’s premium, that one renewal out of three is thin evidence, that partners such as the insurer seek exclusivity and data the company may not be able to give, and that a component supplier often captures little of the value it enables.

perspectives.title: Sell, or take the strategic investment
perspectives.text: An offer at roughly three times invested capital, arriving while growth is slowing and the core technology is commoditizing, may be the best risk-adjusted outcome for investors and employees. A buyer with distribution can do things Ferrovane cannot. The counterarguments are that the offer signals the asset may be worth more, that the minority-investment version gives away exclusivity in markets Ferrovane may need, and that media ownership could damage trust with the elite clients who generate nearly all current revenue. Selling is a strategy only if it follows from a diagnosis, not from fatigue.

case.application: The same fork appears in player development, which repeatedly chooses between depth and breadth. A department can concentrate intensive, individualized programming on a small number of players where its added value is highest, or build scalable systems that reach every player at lower intensity; it can build its own measurement and analysis tools or buy them; and it must decide how players’ data may be used and by whom. Ferrovane’s situation also mirrors a common internal pattern: staff who learn a vendor’s method may later replace the vendor, which is good for the organization’s capability and a warning about where advantage really sits. The disciplined response is the same as Ferrovane’s: diagnose the binding constraint, commit to the few things that define the position, stage what is uncertain, and say plainly what will stop.

questions.prompt: Which statement best captures Porter’s distinction between operational effectiveness and strategy?

options.text: Operational effectiveness concerns cost; strategy concerns growth.

Operational effectiveness means performing similar activities better than rivals; strategy means performing different activities, or similar activities differently, to deliver a distinctive mix of value.
Strategy is set by the board, operational effectiveness by managers.
Operational effectiveness, pursued continuously, is sufficient for sustained advantage.

questions.explanation: Porter defines operational effectiveness as doing similar activities better and strategic positioning as doing different activities or doing them differently. Because best practices diffuse, operational effectiveness is necessary but not sufficient; only a distinctive position, protected by trade-offs and fit, can sustain an advantage.

optionFeedback.a: Both concepts can involve cost. A low-cost position is a strategy; cutting costs with widely available practices is operational effectiveness.
optionFeedback.c: The distinction is about the nature of the activity, not who decides it.
optionFeedback.d: This is precisely what Porter rejects: continuous improvement that rivals can copy leads to convergence, not sustained advantage.

questions.prompt: Which concept best explains the outcome?

stimulus.text: A premium regional airline known for spacious seats and free checked bags launches a “basic” fare on its busiest routes to fight a low-cost entrant. The basic fare uses the same aircraft, crews and airports, removes seat selection and bags, and is sold alongside premium fares. Eighteen months later the airline’s cost per seat is unchanged, premium customers complain about crowded boarding, and the entrant still undercuts it. (Fictional.)

options.text: Straddling: the airline tried to occupy two positions without accepting the trade-offs of either.
Competitive convergence caused by industry-wide benchmarking.
An emergent strategy that leadership failed to recognize.
Insufficient operational effectiveness in the basic-fare operation.

questions.explanation: The airline copied the visible features of the low-cost position (no bags, no seat choice) without the activities that make low costs possible, while degrading its premium offer. Porter calls this straddling: the costs of two positions and the advantages of neither. The low-cost entrant’s advantage rests on a system of trade-offs the incumbent did not accept.

optionFeedback.b: Convergence describes rivals becoming alike through shared practices. Here the airline’s problem is internal incoherence, not imitation of best practice.
optionFeedback.c: The basic fare was a deliberate, intended move, not a pattern that emerged unplanned.
optionFeedback.d: Better execution of the basic fare could not fix a cost structure built for premium service; the problem is positional.

questions.prompt: What is the main flaw in this reasoning?

stimulus.text: “Our strategy for the next three years is to grow revenue 15% a year, reach a 20% operating margin and become the employer of choice in our industry. These goals are ambitious, measurable and each is owned by a named executive. So we have a clear strategy.” (Fictional chief executive.)

options.text: The goals are too ambitious to be credible.
It mistakes goals for strategy: there is no diagnosis of the obstacle and no guiding policy explaining how the goals will be reached or what will be given up.
Strategic goals should not be measurable, because measurement invites gaming.
Assigning goals to individual executives undermines collective accountability.

questions.explanation: Rumelt lists mistaking goals for strategy as a hallmark of bad strategy. Measurable goals are useful, but they describe where you want to end up, not how you will overcome the obstacle in the way. Without a diagnosis and a guiding policy, the statement cannot tell anyone what to do differently or what to stop.

optionFeedback.a: Ambition is not the flaw; even modest goals would not constitute a strategy without a diagnosis and policy.
optionFeedback.c: Measurement can be gamed (Week 8), but the absence of measurement would not turn goals into a strategy.
optionFeedback.d: Named ownership can support accountability; it is not the logical gap in the argument.

questions.prompt: A hospital values Vendor A’s scheduling system at $600,000 a year; A’s suppliers and staff would accept $200,000 a year to provide it. The hospital’s best alternative is Vendor B, which it values at $480,000 a year and whose suppliers and staff would accept $160,000. Using Brandenburger and Stuart’s definitions, what is Vendor A’s added value, in $000 a year?
questions.working: Value created with A = 600 − 200 = 400. Value created without A (the hospital uses B) = 480 − 160 = 320. Added value of A = 400 − 320 = 80.
questions.explanation: Added value is the total value created with the firm minus the total value created without it. Vendor A creates $400,000 of value, but $320,000 could be created without A, so A adds $80,000. Under Brandenburger and Stuart’s assumptions, that caps what A can capture, whatever its current price.

questions.prompt: A start-up sells scheduling software to restaurants. Which of the following are forces — not factors — in Porter’s framework that could limit the start-up’s profitability? Select all that apply.

options.text: Restaurants can switch easily among five similar products.
The restaurant industry is growing quickly.
A payments company now bundles free scheduling with its card terminals.
The government subsidizes restaurant technology purchases.
The software runs on one of only two viable cloud providers, which raises prices every year.
Restaurant staff increasingly use smartphones, a complementary product.

questions.explanation: Easy switching among similar products reflects rivalry and buyer power; a bundled free alternative is a substitute (and a well-resourced entrant); a concentrated cloud provider is supplier power. Industry growth, government policy and complementary products are factors that matter only through their effects on the forces, as Porter emphasizes.

questions.prompt: A board member reads this fictional study and says: “Industry barely matters — only 11%. Strategy explains 38% of profitability, so we can succeed in any industry if our team is strong.” Which interpretation is best supported?

stimulus.text: Fictional study. Researchers decomposed the variance in return on assets of 4,000 business units over ten years.

stimulus.caption: Share of variance in profitability (fictional)
stimulus.note: Synthetic data for a fictional study.

options.text: Only 11% of the company’s future profitability will depend on its industry, so industry choice can be ignored.
The business-specific share proves that strategy causes 38% of profitability.
Because 42% of the variance is unattributed, the study is uninformative and should be disregarded.

The study describes how variance is distributed across many units; it does not show that industry is unimportant for a particular decision, and the business-specific share also includes luck and unmeasured differences.

questions.explanation: Variance decompositions are descriptive. They show how profitability differences line up with industry, parent, year and business across a large sample, not what causes them or how much industry matters for one firm’s choice. The business-specific share is partly a residual that includes luck and measurement differences, and real studies find that industry matters more in some sectors than others.

optionFeedback.a: A share of variance across thousands of units is not a forecast for one company, and industry effects vary greatly by sector.
optionFeedback.b: “Business-specific” is not the same as “strategy”; it includes luck, accounting and anything else particular to the unit. And variance shares are not causal estimates.
optionFeedback.c: A large unexplained share is common and does not make the attributed shares uninformative; it limits how precisely they can be used.

questions.prompt: What is the best next move?

stimulus.text: A national law firm (fictional) is deciding how to obtain artificial-intelligence tools for contract review. Three vendors offer similar tools at competitive prices on one-year terms. The firm’s distinctive strength is its regulatory practice, where partners’ judgment and client relationships command premium fees and where it holds twenty years of annotated regulatory filings. Its eight-person knowledge-management team proposes building a proprietary contract-review model, an 18-month project that would absorb the whole team.

options.text: Build the proprietary model: owning the technology is the only route to sustained advantage.

Buy a vendor tool on short terms with strong data-access and confidentiality provisions, and direct the internal team to integrate it with the regulatory practice’s workflows and its annotated filings.
Sign a five-year exclusive license with one vendor at a premium to deny the tool to rivals.
Wait two years until the market settles before doing anything.

questions.explanation: General contract review is widely available, so building it would spend scarce internal talent on something rivals can buy — competitive parity at best. The differentiating resources are the regulatory practice’s judgment, relationships and annotated filings, which are rare and hard to imitate. Buying the commodity layer and building the integration on top concentrates internal effort where the resource-based view says advantage can arise, while short terms limit vendor hold-up.

optionFeedback.a: Owning technology is not the same as advantage. A model rivals can approximate by buying a similar tool is unlikely to be rare or inimitable, and the build consumes the team for 18 months.
optionFeedback.c: Exclusivity with one of three similar vendors does not make the capability rare — rivals can buy from the other two — and long terms increase hold-up risk.
optionFeedback.d: Waiting forgoes learning and parity benefits; nothing in the scenario suggests the uncertainty will resolve by waiting, and a short-term purchase is easy to reverse.

questions.prompt: Rank these resources from most to least likely to sustain a competitive advantage under Barney’s VRIN criteria.

options.text: A hospital’s infection-control routines, built over a decade across hundreds of staff, which visiting peers have repeatedly failed to replicate
A proprietary dataset that took two years to collect and that rivals could gather in a similar time
A celebrated surgeon recruited last year on a market-rate contract with no restrictions on leaving
A widely available imaging machine bought at list price

questions.explanation: The routines (a) are valuable, rare and protected by social complexity and causal ambiguity, so they are the strongest candidate. The dataset (b) is valuable and rare for now, but imitable within about two years, so it offers a temporary advantage. The surgeon (c) is valuable but mobile: rivals can bid, and the surgeon is likely to capture most of the value through pay. The machine (d) is available to everyone, so it provides parity at most.

questions.prompt: Which explanation is most consistent with this week’s evidence and reasoning?

stimulus.text: Over several seasons, a fictional professional soccer club earned a reputation for signing undervalued players using a proprietary model of chance creation. Its success was widely covered, two of its analysts were hired by rival clubs, and similar models became available from commercial data providers. The owner now asks why the club’s returns in the transfer market have fallen even though its model is more accurate than ever.

options.text: The model was never valid; the early results were luck.
The edge was information-based: as rivals adopted similar methods, the prices of the players the model favored rose toward their value, and the advantage was competed away.
Regression to the mean in player performance fully explains the decline.
The club’s operational effectiveness in scouting declined.

questions.explanation: The stimulus describes the life cycle of an information-based edge: visibility (media coverage), diffusion (analysts hired away, commercial models) and imitation. Once rivals value the same players correctly, those players cost more and the edge disappears even though the model still works. This mirrors Hakes and Sauer’s finding that the undervaluation of on-base skill diminished after the idea became public.

optionFeedback.a: The model’s accuracy has improved, so invalidity is not the best explanation; the pattern points to imitation.
optionFeedback.c: Regression to the mean may contribute to any decline after a strong run, but it does not explain why the decline coincides with rivals adopting the same methods.
optionFeedback.d: Nothing suggests the club’s scouting got worse; the model is more accurate than ever. What changed is the competition.

questions.prompt: A media company can launch a streaming service now for $30M. With probability 0.3 demand is strong and the service is worth $80M; otherwise it is worth $15M. Alternatively, it can spend $3M on a regional pilot that reveals demand and then launch for $30M only if demand is strong. Assuming the pilot delays nothing that matters, by how much does the expected value of staging exceed the expected value of launching now, in $M?
questions.working: Launch now: 0.3 × 80 + 0.7 × 15 − 30 = 24 + 10.5 − 30 = 4.5. Stage: 0.3 × (80 − 30) − 3 = 15 − 3 = 12. Difference: 12 − 4.5 = 7.5. Check: staging avoids the 30 − 15 = 15 loss in the weak state, worth 0.7 × 15 = 10.5, at a cost of 3: 10.5 − 3 = 7.5.
questions.explanation: The pilot is valuable because its result changes the decision: in the weak state the company does not launch. Staging truncates the downside, which is the core intuition of real-options reasoning. The comparison would change if waiting let a rival capture the market first, which is why options thinking supports judgment rather than replacing it.

questions.prompt: As the executive responsible for strategy, what is the best next move?

stimulus.text: A university hospital (fictional) adopts a strategy of becoming the region’s leading center for complex cardiac care. Its capital committee then allocates 22% of the capital budget to cardiac services and spreads the rest across 14 departments in proportion to last year’s budgets. The chief of cardiology says the program needs a second hybrid operating room and twelve more specialist nurses to reach the case volumes at which outcomes and costs improve; the committee says that would be “unfair” to other departments.

options.text: Accept the allocation: proportional budgets maintain morale, and the strategy can be pursued gradually.

Reopen the allocation: show the committee that its realized strategy is proportional spreading, establish the minimum scale the cardiac program needs, and name which departments’ requests will be deferred and why.
Abandon the cardiac strategy, since the organization will not fund it.
Fund the cardiac request by cutting every other department by the same percentage.

questions.explanation: The stated strategy and the realized allocation contradict each other, and the cardiac program has a minimum scale below which the strategy cannot work. Making the contradiction explicit, establishing the threshold and choosing deliberately what to defer turns a budget into a strategy. It is also the politically harder option, which is why it so rarely happens.

optionFeedback.a: Funding the strategy below its minimum scale is likely to produce neither the strategy nor savings; “gradually” can mean never.
optionFeedback.c: Abandoning the strategy may be right if the diagnosis was wrong, but the problem described is the allocation, not the diagnosis.
optionFeedback.d: Equal cuts are peanut-butter allocation in reverse: they avoid choosing which activities matter less and may damage departments that support the cardiac program.

questions.prompt: Write a strategy kernel for a fictional organization of your choice (120–180 words): a diagnosis of its critical challenge, a guiding policy and two or three coherent actions. End with one thing the organization will stop doing and why.
questions.modelAnswer: Organization: a fictional regional children’s hospital. Diagnosis: the hospital’s specialty clinics have six-month waits because pediatric specialists spend about a third of their time on follow-up visits that nurse practitioners could handle; families leave for distant academic centers, taking referrals and research volume with them. Guiding policy: compete on timely access to specialty care for the region’s families, using specialists only where their expertise is decisive. Coherent actions: (1) create nurse-practitioner-led follow-up clinics with clear escalation rules; (2) give regional pediatricians a same-week electronic consultation service; (3) report access times publicly by specialty each quarter. Stop: the planned expansion into adult outpatient imaging, which would compete for the same capital and leadership attention without addressing the access problem.

rubric.criterion: Diagnosis names a specific, causal challenge (not a goal or slogan) that could be checked
levels: 0 — a goal, aspiration or vague statement
1 — a challenge is named but its cause is unclear
2 — a specific obstacle with a plausible causal explanation

rubric.criterion: Guiding policy channels action and rules out attractive alternatives
levels: 1 — an approach is stated but rules nothing out
2 — a clear approach that implies trade-offs

rubric.criterion: Actions are coherent with the policy and each other, and the stop item follows from the diagnosis
levels: 0 — unrelated list or no stop item
1 — actions fit but the stop item is generic
2 — reinforcing actions and a concrete, costly stop item tied to the diagnosis

reserve.prompt: Why does fit among activities make a strategic position harder to imitate?

options.text: Because fit makes each activity individually superior to a rival’s.
Because rivals must replicate a whole system of mutually reinforcing activities, and the chance of matching all of them is much lower than the chance of matching any one.
Because fit always produces lower costs than rivals have.
Because activities that fit together are legally protected.

reserve.explanation: Porter argues that the value of a strategy lies in the system of activities, not in any single practice. If each activity has some chance of not being copied successfully, the probability of copying the whole system multiplies down quickly. That is why a rival can match a practice but still fail to match the position.

optionFeedback.a: Activities in a well-fitting system need not be individually best-in-class; their value comes from how they reinforce one another.
optionFeedback.c: Fit can support differentiation as well as low cost; it does not always lower costs.
optionFeedback.d: Fit has nothing to do with legal protection.

reserve.prompt: A customer’s willingness to pay is 250, the price is 180, the firm’s cost is 120 and the suppliers’ opportunity cost is 90 (all in $000). What percentage of the value created does the firm capture?
reserve.working: Value created = 250 − 90 = 160. Firm captures price − cost = 180 − 120 = 60. Share = 60 ÷ 160 = 0.375 = 37.5%. (Customer keeps 70, suppliers keep 30.)
reserve.explanation: Value created is fixed by the two ends of the value line — willingness to pay and suppliers’ opportunity cost. Price and cost divide it among customer, firm and suppliers. The firm’s 60 is its share of a 160 total.

reserve.prompt: What is the main flaw in this reasoning?

stimulus.text: “Our hospital ranks first in the region for cardiac outcomes, and we bought the newest imaging system three years ago. Since the imaging system is associated with our best-in-region outcomes, it must be our source of sustained advantage, and we should double the imaging budget.” (Fictional executive.)

options.text: It labels a resource valuable because of the success it is meant to explain, and ignores that rivals can buy the same machine; the advantage more plausibly rests on rarer, harder-to-copy resources such as team routines.
Its sample is too small to support any conclusion.
Cardiac outcomes are not a valid measure of hospital performance.
It implies the hospital should cut imaging, which would harm patients.

reserve.explanation: The argument is the after-the-fact reasoning that Priem and Butler warned about: success is used to certify a resource as valuable. A purchasable machine also fails the rarity test, because rivals can buy it. Under the resource-based view, sustained advantage is more likely to come from socially complex routines that rivals cannot buy.

optionFeedback.b: Sample size is a concern in many arguments, but the core flaw here is circular attribution and the neglect of rarity.
optionFeedback.c: Outcomes are a reasonable measure; the flaw is in attributing them to one purchasable resource.
optionFeedback.d: The argument recommends more imaging, not less; the flaw is in its logic, not its recommendation’s direction.

reserve.prompt: Which of the following are signs that an organization’s realized strategy differs from its stated strategy? Select all that apply.

options.text: Budget increases are spread evenly across all units despite a stated focus on two of them.
The strategy’s priority initiative is staffed by people lent part-time from other teams.
A program the strategy said would end still receives its full budget.
Leaders refer to the strategy in every all-staff meeting.
The priority initiative received a larger share of capital than last year.
A pilot was stopped after missing a threshold agreed before it started.

reserve.explanation: Realized strategy shows up in commitments of money, people and attention. Even spreading, part-time staffing of a priority and continued funding of a program meant to end all reveal a pattern different from the plan. Talking about the strategy, shifting capital toward the priority, and stopping a pilot by a pre-agreed rule are consistent with the stated strategy.

assignment.title: The Strategy Memo

brief.text: Write a strategy memo for a fictional sports or technology organization that faces resource constraints and competing priorities. You may use Ferrovane Labs from this week’s case, or design your own fictional organization — for example, a sports-technology start-up, a professional soccer academy, a collegiate athletics department, a streaming platform or a software company. Do not use a real organization, and do not use confidential information from any workplace. If you invent figures, label them synthetic and state your assumptions.

Your reader is a board or ownership group of five people who will read the memo before a sixty-minute meeting. They are intelligent, busy and skeptical. They do not need a tour of frameworks; they need a diagnosis they can test, a policy they can hold you to, and a clear account of what the strategy will cost — including what the organization will stop doing.

items: Use Rumelt’s kernel as the spine: diagnosis, guiding policy, coherent actions.

Show where the organization’s advantage will come from: a position with trade-offs (Lesson 1), a market position where it can capture value (Lesson 2), or resources and capabilities rivals cannot easily copy (Lesson 3) — or a combination.
Translate the strategy into resources: what gets funded, what gets less, what stops. A strategy that costs nothing is not a strategy.
Name the leading indicators that would tell you within six to twelve months whether the strategy is working, and the evidence that would make you change course.
Separate evidence from assumption. Where you rely on research, cite it; where you rely on judgment or synthetic data, say so.

brief.text: The memo’s structure follows Rumelt’s kernel, extended with the resource and monitoring sections an executive audience expects. The frameworks are practitioner tools and conceptual arguments, not validated predictive models; use them to discipline your reasoning, not to decorate it.

assignment.deliverable: A 1,000–1,500-word strategy memo with a diagnosis, guiding policy, coherent actions, resource implications, a stop-doing list, leading indicators and risks.

template.heading: Diagnosis
template.guidance: Name the critical challenge and explain its causes in three to five sentences. Cite the evidence (case exhibits, synthetic data you have labelled, or research) and say what would show the diagnosis is wrong.

template.heading: Guiding policy
template.guidance: State the overall approach in one or two sentences. Make clear which attractive options it rules out and where the organization’s advantage will come from.

template.heading: Coherent actions
template.guidance: List three to five actions that carry out the policy and reinforce each other. For each, say how it connects to the diagnosis.

template.heading: Resource implications
template.guidance: Show how money, people and leadership attention shift: what gets more, what gets less, what is staged as an option and what triggers further investment.

template.heading: What we will stop doing
template.guidance: Name at least two specific activities, products, programs or customers the organization will stop or decline, and the cost of stopping each.

template.heading: Leading indicators
template.guidance: Give three to five measurable indicators that would signal within six to twelve months whether the strategy is working, with the threshold that would prompt a change.

template.heading: Risks and what would change our mind
template.guidance: Identify the two or three most important risks, including competitors’ likely responses, and the evidence that would lead you to revise the strategy.

rubric.criterion: Diagnosis: identifies a specific, causal and testable critical challenge supported by evidence

levels.label: Exemplary
levels.descriptor: A precise, causal diagnosis that explains why the obvious options are insufficient; evidence is cited and its limits acknowledged; states what would falsify it.

levels.label: Proficient
levels.descriptor: A clear diagnosis with plausible causes and supporting evidence; limits partly acknowledged.

levels.label: Developing
levels.descriptor: A challenge is named but is partly a goal or symptom; causes or evidence are thin.

levels.label: Beginning
levels.descriptor: No real diagnosis: restates goals, aspirations or a list of problems.

rubric.criterion: Guiding policy and coherence: the policy channels action, implies trade-offs and the actions reinforce each other

levels.label: Exemplary
levels.descriptor: A sharp policy that rules out attractive alternatives; every action follows from it and the actions reinforce one another; the source of advantage is explicit.

levels.label: Proficient
levels.descriptor: A clear policy and actions that fit it, with minor gaps in coherence or in the account of advantage.

levels.label: Developing
levels.descriptor: A policy is stated but rules little out, or several actions do not follow from it.

levels.label: Beginning
levels.descriptor: No guiding policy, or a list of unrelated initiatives.

rubric.criterion: Resource realism and opportunity cost: allocation, staging and what stops

levels.label: Exemplary
levels.descriptor: Resources visibly follow the strategy; staged options and triggers are specified; at least two costly, concrete stop items are justified by the diagnosis.

levels.label: Proficient
levels.descriptor: Resource shifts are clear and a credible stop list is given, with some staging logic.

levels.label: Developing
levels.descriptor: Resources are mentioned but not reallocated, or the stop list is generic or costless.

levels.label: Beginning
levels.descriptor: No resource implications or nothing stops; the strategy is free.

rubric.criterion: Indicators, risks and uncertainty: leading indicators, competitive responses and conditions for changing course

levels.label: Exemplary
levels.descriptor: Measurable leading indicators with thresholds; key risks include competitors’ responses; clear conditions for revising the strategy.

levels.label: Proficient
levels.descriptor: Relevant indicators and risks; some thresholds or change conditions are missing.

levels.label: Developing
levels.descriptor: Indicators are lagging or vague; risks are generic.

levels.label: Beginning
levels.descriptor: No indicators or risks.

levels.label: Exemplary
levels.descriptor: Synthetic figures and assumptions are labelled; research is cited accurately and not overstated; recommendation is clear in the opening paragraph; concise and readable for a board.

levels.label: Proficient
levels.descriptor: Mostly well labelled and clearly written; minor overstatement or length issues.

levels.label: Developing
levels.descriptor: Assumptions and evidence are blurred, or the recommendation is buried.

levels.label: Beginning
levels.descriptor: Claims are unsupported or overstated; hard to follow.

scenario.text: You are drafting a strategy memo for the board of a fictional sports or technology organization — Ferrovane Labs from this week’s case, or one of your own design. The board meets in a week. It has asked for a recommendation it can test, the resources it will require and what the organization will stop doing.

audience.cares: Return on capital, runway, a credible path to scale or an exit, and whether the team is choosing rather than hedging.

audience.who: Independent board member with operating experience
audience.cares: Whether the diagnosis is right, whether the organization has the capabilities the strategy requires, and execution risk.
Whether the strategy is coherent, what it asks of their units, and how the stop list will be explained to staff and clients.

formats.label: Strategy memo
sections: Risks and what would change our mind

checklist: The recommendation appears in the first two sentences.
The diagnosis names a cause, not a goal.
The guiding policy rules out at least one attractive option.
Every action connects to the diagnosis.
At least two specific things stop, with their cost.
Leading indicators have thresholds and dates.
Synthetic numbers and assumptions are labelled as such.

prompts: Think of the last plan you contributed to. Write its kernel as it actually was — diagnosis, guiding policy, coherent actions. Which element was missing or weakest, and why do you think it was left out?
Name one edge an organization you know well has relied on that is based mainly on information or method. How visible is it now, and what would remain if rivals copied it tomorrow?
If you were accountable for the whole budget of your area, what is one activity, program or commitment you would stop? What makes stopping it hard — evidence, politics or identity?
Where do you tend to err: committing too early, or staging and hedging too long? Recall a specific decision and what it cost.

review.front: Operational effectiveness versus strategic positioning: what is the difference, and why does it matter?
review.back: Operational effectiveness is doing similar activities better; positioning is doing different activities or doing them differently. Effectiveness diffuses and rivals converge, so it rarely sustains an advantage; a position protected by trade-offs and fit can.

review.front: What is straddling, and why does it fail?
review.back: Trying to occupy two incompatible positions at once — e.g. a full-service airline adding a low-fare service on the same system. It carries the costs of both positions and the advantages of neither.

review.front: Why does fit among activities protect a position?
review.back: Rivals must copy a whole system of reinforcing activities, not one practice; the probability of matching every element multiplies down quickly.

review.front: Name the three parts of Rumelt’s kernel and two hallmarks of bad strategy.
review.back: Diagnosis, guiding policy, coherent actions. Hallmarks of bad strategy: fluff, failure to face the challenge, mistaking goals for strategy, bad strategic objectives.

review.front: Define opportunity cost and give the question it adds to every proposal.
review.back: The value of the best alternative forgone. It changes “Is this good?” into “Is this better than what we would do with the same money, people and attention instead?”
Threat of new entrants, bargaining power of suppliers, bargaining power of buyers, threat of substitutes, rivalry among existing competitors.

review.front: Is industry growth one of the five forces?
review.back: No. Growth, technology, government and complements are factors that matter only through their effects on the five forces; rapid growth can attract entrants.

review.front: How is value created defined in value-based strategy, and how is it divided?
review.back: Willingness to pay minus suppliers’ opportunity cost. Customers keep WTP − price, the firm keeps price − cost, suppliers keep cost − opportunity cost.

review.front: What is added value, and why does it matter?
review.back: Total value created with a player minus total value created without it. A firm cannot capture more than its added value, so it tells you how much of today’s margin is defensible.

review.front: What did McGahan and Porter (1997) find about industry and firm effects, and what is the main caution?
review.back: Roughly 19% of variance in business-unit profitability was associated with industry and 32% with business-specific effects (corporate parent about 4%, year about 2%), with industry mattering more in services. The figures are descriptive, not causal, and vary by sample and method.

review.front: What do the letters VRIN stand for, and what are Barney’s three sources of imperfect imitability?
review.back: Valuable, rare, imperfectly imitable, non-substitutable. Unique historical conditions, causal ambiguity, social complexity.

review.front: State the tautology critique of the resource-based view and how to avoid it in practice.
review.back: If “valuable” means “produces advantage”, saying valuable resources produce advantage is true by definition (Priem and Butler). Define value from customers and costs before the fact and specify what blocks imitation.
A firm’s ability to integrate, build and reconfigure internal and external competences to address rapidly changing environments (Teece, Pisano and Shuen); shaped by processes, positions and paths.

review.front: Build-versus-buy heuristic: what should you buy and what should you build?
review.back: Buy what is widely available and does not differentiate; build or protect what differentiates, often the integration, data and routines on top of bought tools. Check hold-up risk, learning and opportunity cost.

review.front: What did Hakes and Sauer (2006) find, and what is the strategic lesson?
review.back: On-base skill was undervalued in baseball’s labor market relative to its contribution to winning before the book appeared, and the undervaluation diminished afterward. Information-based edges erode once visible.

review.front: Why can a pilot be worth more than its own returns, and when does staging stop making sense?
review.back: It buys information that changes the decision, cutting off the downside. Staging loses its appeal when waiting lets rivals preempt, or when commitment itself has strategic value.
